column18: The paper proposes a novel self-verifying/self-correcting framework for LLM-based generation of solver-compatible optimization formulations and evaluates it via controlled computational experiments in an artificial (lab) setting, not in operational practice. Section 4 (Experimental Setup and Evaluation) defines the system components (Gurobot LLM generator via Gurobi Portal, Gurobi Optimizer, ROS 2-based simulation) and a defined evaluation protocol with metrics (Section 4.3); Section 5.1 reports quantitative results over 5 trials (zero-shot: 179-417 mismatched constraints; one-shot: 39-59). No real organization, real users, or operational deployment are involved - the conclusion (Section 6) explicitly defers 'validation under conditions closer to actual production environments, as well as experiments with a real robot' to future work. Hence validation-research rather than evaluation-research (not naturalistic/industrial) or solution-proposal (a thorough experimental evaluation is present).
column20: A working system is implemented and evaluated under a defined protocol with defined metrics. Section 4.1 lists concrete implemented components ('LLM generator: Gurobot...; Optimization solver:... Gurobi...; Simulation:... ROS 2-based simulation'), and Table 2 records the concrete environment (Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, AMD Ryzen 5 7530U, ROS 2 Humble, 1278 binary variables, 1362 constraints, 5 trials). Section 4.3 defines four evaluation metrics: (i) effect of prompting strategy via initial mismatch count, (ii) Mode A error detectability via mismatch counts and diagnostic categories, (iii) correction effectiveness via mismatch reduction after feedback-based regeneration, (iv) Mode B task-level simulation results and failure reasons. Section 5.1 reports quantitative outcomes ('Under zero-shot prompting, the number of mismatched constraints ranged from 179 to 417, whereas one-shot prompting reduced this range to 39-59'), and Section 6 confirms Mode B validation ran ('representative optimization outputs were mapped to the ROS 2 / MoveIt Task Constructor environment, and both executable and non-executable cases were identified through task-level validation'). Prototype + controlled evaluation with defined metrics -> implemented-validated.
column22: The paper is explicitly situated in manufacturing. Section 1 opens: 'Recent manufacturing sites have faced a growing need to reconfigure production systems in response to high-mix, low-volume production and changing requirements' and discusses 'robotic production lines'; Section 2 frames the problem 'in a workspace such as a table and/or a conveyor in manufacturing environment'; Section 1 also states 'For LLM-assisted formulation to be used in robotic manufacturing...'. The application domain is robotic manufacturing/production-line design.
column23: Robotic equipment selection and layout planning for pick-and-place operations
column24: Table 2 (Section 4) states Problem type = 'Robotic equipment selection and layout planning' and Target task = 'Robotic pick-and-place operation'. Section 2 describes the case: selecting one robot arm (10 candidates), one gripper (8 candidates), and one workpiece (10 candidates), choosing an installation point from 125 candidate points (22 valid), and assigning 9 placement slots, subject to reachability, collision avoidance, safety-distance, payload/grasp capability, and task-feasibility constraints. The reference MIP formulation comprises 1278 binary variables and 1362 constraints (Section 2, Table 2).
column26: No explicit research questions (RQ1/RQ2-style) are stated anywhere in the paper. The closest analogues are the four contributions listed at the end of Section 1 and the four evaluation aspects in Section 4.3 ('the effect of prompting strategy...; error detectability in Mode A...; correction effectiveness...; and Mode B validation...'), which function as evaluation objectives rather than formally stated research questions. Hence NR.
column28: The paper's two core tasks are equipment selection and layout planning for a robotic pick-and-place workcell (title; §1; §2). Layout planning — choosing a robot installation point from 125 candidate points and assigning workpiece placement slots (§2; Table 1) — maps to factory-planning, since layout planning of production equipment/workpieces is a factory-planning activity (corresponding task: 'factory-layout-planning'). Equipment selection — choosing one robot arm (10 candidates), one gripper (8), and one workpiece (10) with weighted-cost minimization (§2: 'minimize the weighted cost of the selected equipment') — maps to technology-selection. Boundary case (?): the planning object is a single workcell (table/conveyor workspace), not an entire factory, so factory-planning applies at the workcell/line-layout level rather than greenfield factory level. Site-selection does not apply (the installation-point choice is micro-level layout, not facility location); no SC-network, logistics, or GPN aspects are addressed. Evidence: title; §1; §2; Table 1.
column30: Equipment selection from candidate sets for a robotic pick-and-place workcell: selecting one robot arm (from 10 candidates), one gripper (from 8), and one workpiece (from 10) under equipment-capability constraints (payload, gripper opening, gripping force) with weighted equipment-cost minimization (§2; Table 1).
column31: factory-layout-planning: the method determines the robot installation location from 125 predefined candidate points and assigns placement slots to the workpiece (§2; Table 1 variables Y(i), Z(i,j); title 'Layout Planning'). other: equipment selection is a second core task (title; §2 'selecting a robot arm and a gripper from candidates'; Table 1 variables X_r, X_h, X_w) and is not covered by the listed categories — 'technology-scouting' denotes scouting/identification of technologies rather than optimal selection from a given candidate set, 'investment-appraisal' denotes financial evaluation rather than cost-minimizing selection, and 'capacity-dimensioning' concerns resource quantities rather than specific equipment models. Uncertainty (?): if Appendix A maps technology/equipment choice to 'technology-scouting' or 'production-system-concept-design', that would be the alternative coding. Evidence: title; §1; §2; Table 1.
column33: The decision concerns the production process: it selects production equipment (robot arm, gripper) and arranges the workspace of a robotic production line for pick-and-place operations (§1: 'In robotic production lines in particular, decisions such as selecting robot arms and grippers and determining the placement of robots and workpieces...'; §2). No procurement/sourcing, distribution, or sales processes are addressed. Evidence: §1; §2.
column35: The supported decisions fix concrete equipment (specific robot arm/gripper/workpiece models from candidate sets) and a fine-grained layout (one installation point out of 125 candidates; assignment of 9 placement slots), with the solution validated for physical executability and considered 'deployable in a real production environment' (Fig. 1; §2; Table 1). This corresponds to Phase 4 detailed planning (Detailplanung), where equipment and the detailed layout are specified. Uncertainty (?): the paper does not cite VDI 5200, layout planning also appears in Phase 3 concept planning (layout variants), and the planning object is a workcell rather than a whole factory; the phase is therefore inferred from the granularity and implementability of the decisions. Evidence: §2; Table 1; Fig. 1.
column37: No time horizon is stated anywhere in the paper (searched title and §1–§6): the problem is a one-off equipment-selection and layout-design decision, and no planning period, term, or horizon (e.g., 'X years', 'long-term') is mentioned. Evidence: full text.
column40: Strategic: the decision determines what exists in the production system — which equipment is selected and where it is installed/placed — i.e., a system-configuring design decision (§2: 'The objective is to determine a combination of equipment and a layout that makes it possible for the task to be performed safely and stably under the given conditions.'), so the Strategic tier applies. No tactical (mid-term allocation of existing resources) or operational (short-term scheduling/control) decisions are produced; the ROS2/MoveIt pick-and-place simulation in Mode B only validates the physical executability of the design solution and does not schedule or control operations (§3; Fig. 1; §6). Evidence: §2; §3; Fig. 1; §6.
column42: No claim found: the authors never apply the labels 'strategic', 'tactical', or 'operational' to the planning decision or its horizon anywhere in the paper; they speak of 'design work', 'reconfigure production systems', and 'decisions' without a horizon-tier label (the phrase 'operational conditions' in the Abstract refers to task operating conditions, not operational planning). Evidence: Abstract; §1–§6.
column44: The supported decision fixes the physical configuration of the robotic workcell — which equipment exists (selected robot arm, gripper, workpiece) and where it is located (installation point, placement slots) — rather than how existing resources are used. §2: 'The decision-making includes selecting a robot arm and a gripper from candidates, choosing a robot installation location from predefined candidate points, and deciding where to place the workpiece on the table from candidate positions.' Evidence: §2; Table 1.
column46: §2: 'The objective is to determine a combination of equipment and a layout that makes it possible for the task to be performed safely and stably under the given conditions.' This explicitly frames the decision as determining equipment and layout, i.e., configuring system elements. Reinforced by §1: 'decisions such as selecting robot arms and grippers and determining the placement of robots and workpieces are closely related not only to productivity but also to safety.' Evidence: §1; §2.
column47: The decision determines the selected equipment (one robot arm from 10 candidates, one gripper from 8, one workpiece from 10), the robot installation point (one of 125 candidate points), and the assignment of placement slots for the workpiece (9 slots), thereby fixing the equipment set and physical layout of the robotic pick-and-place workcell (§2; Table 1).
column49: The paper uses no planning-domain framework to structure its scope: VDI 5200, the Supply Chain Planning Matrix, Lanza et al. (2019), Wiendahl-Nyhuis, and Melo et al. (2009) are neither cited nor applied, and no other planning reference model (e.g., Systematic Layout Planning) appears. The scope is structured by the MIP problem statement (1278 binary variables, 1362 constraints; §2; Table 1) and the LLM generation–verification–correction workflow (Gurobot, Gurobi, ROS2/MoveIt Task Constructor; §3–§4), which are general methods, not planning-domain frameworks; cited works concern LLM-based optimization modeling (OptiMUS, LM4OPT, NL4Opt; §1). Evidence: §1–§4.
column50: No planning-domain framework is cited or applied. The planning scope is defined solely by the equipment-selection/layout-planning problem statement, its binary-variable MIP formulation, and the LLM-based formulation-generation and validation workflow; mathematical programming, prompt engineering, and simulation-based validation are general methods and therefore do not count as planning-domain reference frameworks.
column52: The paper proposes a self-verifying and self-correcting framework in which an LLM (Gurobot) acts as a formulation assistant - explicitly not a decision maker or source of guaranteed correctness - for robotic equipment selection and layout planning in pick-and-place operations. Input: natural-language specifications of the production environment, candidate robot arms/grippers/workpieces, candidate installation points and placement slots, a weighted cost objective, and constraint categories (reachability, collision avoidance, safety distance, equipment capability such as payload/gripping force, task feasibility), organized into structured prompt sections with example formulations. Output: a solver-compatible Gurobi .lp file (MIP formulation with binary decision variables; reference setting: 1278 variables, 1362 constraints), solved by Gurobi to yield a candidate equipment selection and layout. Decision-support function: generated formulations are never accepted as-is. Mode A (reference formulation available, benchmark evaluation): a constraint-level comparison tool identifies missing/extra/inconsistent constraints and returns a structured discrepancy report to the LLM via API for iterative self-correction. Mode B (no reference formulation): the solution is validated for physical executability (collision check, reachability/workspace constraints, pick-and-place motion feasibility) in a ROS 2/MoveIt Task Constructor simulation; solutions passing all checks are considered deployable in a real production environment.
column54: Gurobot, accessed via the Gurobi Portal chat interface, is the only LLM deployed and evaluated with the paper's own method (§4.1 System Components; Table 2 'LLM generator: Gurobot via the Gurobi Portal chat interface'). Its underlying base model and version are not disclosed ('LLM inference was performed on the service provider side, and the server-side CPU and GPU specifications were not available to the authors', §4.1). No alternative LLMs are run with the method; comparing multiple LLMs is explicitly listed as future work (§6). OptiMUS, LM4OPT and the NL4Opt benchmark are cited only as related work/prior studies (§1), not deployed. The AI Assistance Declaration states generative AI was used solely for language editing of the manuscript, not in the method.
column55: Gurobot is the sole LLM and performs both initial formulation generation from the natural-language specification and regeneration from discrepancy-report feedback; no other LLM is deployed (comparison of multiple LLMs is future work, §6).
column57: Gurobot is Gurobi's own LLM assistant service; the paper never discloses the underlying model family (§3, §4.1, Table 2), so it cannot be mapped to any listed family (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, etc.) and is coded 'other'.
column58: Gurobot - Gurobi's proprietary LLM-based optimization-modeling assistant accessed via the Gurobi Portal chat interface; underlying model family not disclosed in the paper.
column60: Gurobot is a proprietary hosted service: Table 2 lists 'LLM generator: Gurobot via the Gurobi Portal chat interface' and §4.1 states that LLM inference was performed on the service provider side. No open weights are available for this deployed service, so 'N'.
column63: §4.1/Table 2: 'Gurobot was accessed through the Gurobi Portal chat interface. Therefore, LLM inference was performed on the service provider side.' The local machine (Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, AMD Ryzen 5 7530U, 7 GiB RAM) was used only for file handling, constraint-level verification, solver execution and ROS 2 simulation - not for LLM inference. Hence 'API'.
column65: The LLM receives natural-language text only: specifications organized into sections ('environment', 'candidates', 'objective', 'constraints'), expected variable domains, example formulations, and textual discrepancy reports returned for correction (§3.1-§3.2). No image or other modality is fed to the LLM; the ROS 2/MoveIt simulation validates solutions downstream and is not LLM input. Hence 'text'.
column67: No weight updates or fine-tuning of any kind are described; the method relies entirely on prompt design (structured input sections, one-shot examples) and feedback-based regeneration (§3.2, contribution 2). Hence 'none'.
column71: §3.2: input requirements are organized into structured sections, the prompt specifies expected variable domains for major decision types, and the LLM must output a solver-compatible .lp file - output constrained to a formal format, coded structured-output. §3.2: 'a small number of example formulations are given in advance' - few-shot (one-shot) prompting. §5.1/Fig. 2: zero-shot and one-shot prompting are both run with the same framework (zero-shot as baseline condition, one-shot as the stabilized setting; mismatch counts 179-417 vs 39-59), so both are coded. No CoT, self-consistency or ReAct is described.
column74: The framework is a developer-fixed workflow (Fig. 1, §3): Gurobot generates the .lp file, Gurobi solves it, and deterministic components (LP Constraint Comparison Tool in Mode A; ROS 2/MoveIt simulation in Mode B) validate the result, with discrepancy reports fed back to the same LLM for regeneration. There is only one LLM role (formulation generator); the LLM neither decides its next action nor calls tools at run time. Per the schema, an LLM used as a single generator function inside conventional software - even with a deterministic validation feedback loop - is 'none'; 'pipeline' would require several specialised LLM roles, which do not exist here.
column76: The only loop is: LLM generates formulation -> deterministic validation (LP Constraint Comparison Tool / Gurobi solver / ROS 2 MoveIt simulation) -> structured discrepancy report returned to the generating LLM -> regeneration (Fig. 1, §3, §6). Per the schema (0.10.4), feedback from deterministic code to the generating LLM is not evaluator-optimizer, and such loops fall under 'none'. There are no two LLM calls with distinct roles, no routing, no parallel LLM calls and no orchestrator. Hence 'none'.
column80: agent_memory = short-term: within a correction session the LLM receives the structured discrepancy report (and prior formulation context) and regenerates based on it - working memory/conversation history within one task (§3.2 'reports obtained from the verification modules are returned to the LLM, and the generated formulation is regenerated based on that feedback'; §6 'returned to the LLM through an API so that the formulation can be revised iteratively'); no persistent long-term memory across tasks is described (? exact context management not detailed). planning_reflection = false: the LLM does not plan or self-critique; all critique comes from external deterministic tools, and the 'self-correcting' loop is framework-driven rather than LLM self-reflection. tool_use = false: the LLM does not decide tool calls at run time; the generate -> solve -> verify -> simulate sequence is fixed by the developer (Fig. 1, §3, §4.1).
column82: solver: the LLM-generated .lp files are solved with the Gurobi Optimizer to obtain candidate solutions (§3.3, §4.1, Table 2 'Solver: Gurobi Optimizer'). simulation-platform: in Mode B (no reference formulation) the obtained solution is applied to a ROS 2 (Humble)/MoveIt Task Constructor simulation to evaluate collision, reachability/workspace and pick-and-place motion feasibility (§1, §3, Fig. 1, §4.1, §6). The Mode A 'LP Constraint Comparison Tool' is a custom deterministic verification component internal to the framework with no matching enum category. No RAG, non-LLM ML model, digital twin, code execution, database/SQL, enterprise system, CAD/GIS or web-search integration is described.
column84: The proposed method itself formulates and solves an optimization problem: the LLM (Gurobot) generates a solver-compatible .lp file representing a MIP for equipment selection and layout planning (1278 binary variables, 1362 constraints), which is then solved by Gurobi to obtain candidate solutions (§1 contributions, §2, §3.3, §4.1, Table 2). This is exactly the 'LLM-generated model that is then solved' case; optimization is the core of the method, not merely background or a comparison baseline.
column86: High: §2 and Table 1 explicitly define the decision variables (binary X_r(k), X_h(k), X_w(k) for robot/gripper/workpiece selection, Y(i) for installation-point selection, Z_{i,j} for placement-slot assignment; 1278 binary variables in total), a linear objective (minimize the weighted cost of the selected robot arm, gripper, and workpiece via coefficients C_r(k), C_h(k), C_w(k)), and 1362 constraints (selection of one robot/gripper/workpiece/installation point, gripper opening, robot payload, gripper payload, gripping force, candidate-point validity, assignment, reachability). The explicit mathematical program is solved exactly by Gurobi Optimizer (§4.1, Table 2).
column88: MILP-LP: the formulation is 'linear in its objective function and constraints' with binary decision variables — 'Linear optimization formulation with binary decision variables in Gurobi-compatible .lp format' (Table 2); the paper also states such problems are 'naturally modeled as MIP problems' (§1). The ROS2/MoveIt Task Constructor simulation in Mode B is used only to validate physical executability (collision, reachability, pick-and-place feasibility) of the Gurobi solution (§3, Fig. 1, §6); it does not drive the search, so simulation-optimization does not apply. No stochastic, metaheuristic, RL, CP, NLP, or MCDM elements are present.
column91: Formulator: Gurobot translates the natural-language specification (environment, candidates, objective, constraints) into the solver-compatible .lp model itself — decision variables, objective function, and constraints (§3.1, §3.3) — and, in the self-correction loop, revises the LP formulation based on the structured discrepancy report returned via API (§1, §3.2, Fig. 1, §6), i.e., its output is the model or a change to it. The LLM does not call the solver as a tool (Gurobi is executed locally by the framework: Table 2 'Local environment usage: ... solver execution'; LLM inference is server-side via Gurobi Portal), does not write solver-invoking code (it writes the .lp model file directly), does not propose/improve solutions itself (candidate solutions come from Gurobi), and does not verify (the LP Constraint Comparison Tool and the ROS2/MoveIt simulation perform the checking and issue the reports), so no other role applies.
column93: Table 2 lists 'Solver: Gurobi Optimizer'; §4.1 states 'The generated solver-compatible .lp files are solved with Gurobi to obtain candidate solutions'; the .lp file format is Gurobi's (Abstract, §1).
column94: Equipment selection and layout planning for a robotic pick-and-place task, formulated as a linear optimization model with binary decision variables (MIP) in Gurobi-compatible .lp format. Decision variables (Table 1): X_r(k) selects one robot arm from 10 candidates; X_h(k) selects one gripper from 8; X_w(k) selects one workpiece from 10; Y(i) selects one installation point from 125 candidates (22 valid); Z_{i,j} assigns candidate points to 9 placement slots — 1278 binary variables in total. Objective: minimize the weighted cost of the selected equipment (cost coefficients C_r(k), C_h(k), C_w(k) for robot arm, gripper, and workpiece). Constraints (1362 total): selection of exactly one robot arm, gripper, workpiece, and valid installation point; equipment capability constraints (gripper opening width vs. workpiece diameter, robot payload, gripper payload, gripping force); candidate-point validity; assignment; and reachability. The LLM-generated .lp file is solved by Gurobi; the solution is then validated either by constraint-level comparison against a reference formulation with iterative LLM self-correction (Mode A) or by ROS2/MoveIt Task Constructor simulation checking physical executability of the pick-and-place task (Mode B).
column96: The paper's own method is evaluated on a single author-constructed case - robotic pick-and-place equipment selection and layout planning (Sections 2, 4.1, Table 2) - worked through in Mode A (constraint-level comparison against a reference formulation) and Mode B (ROS 2/MoveIt simulation validation), fitting 'single-case'. The zero-shot vs one-shot prompting comparison is a controlled comparison of two conditions on the same task/problem setting (Sections 4.3(i), 5.1, Fig. 2), fitting 'quasi-experimental'. No user study, field deployment, or multiple distinct cases are present; the 5 Mode A trials repeat the same problem setting ('All five trials used the same problem setting', Section 4.1), so this is not a test-set of distinct items.
column98: All evaluation episodes are artificial: the problem instance (candidate robots/grippers/workpieces, installation points, placement slots) is constructed by the authors, the reference formulation is author-prepared and explicitly used 'only as a controlled benchmark' (Section 1), and Mode B feasibility/safety checks run in a ROS 2/MoveIt Task Constructor simulation environment (Sections 1, 3, 4.1, 6). No real organisation, real operational data, or real users are involved; real-robot and real-production validation is listed as future work (Section 6).
column100: No public dataset or benchmark is used for evaluation. The evaluation relies on an author-constructed problem instance (10 robot-arm, 8 gripper, 10 workpiece candidates; 125 installation candidate points of which 22 valid; 9 placement slots; 1278 binary variables; 1362 constraints) with an author-prepared reference formulation serving as a controlled benchmark (Sections 1-2, Table 2). NL4Opt and other benchmarks are mentioned only as related work (Section 1), not used for evaluation.
column102: No alternative method is applied to the same task and case. The zero-shot vs one-shot comparison (Section 5.1) is an ablation of the method's own prompting component (contribution 2, Section 1), and Mode A's constraint-level comparison against the reference formulation is comparison against ground truth; per the schema, neither counts as a comparator. No human-planner, conventional-method, or prior-AI-ML baseline is evaluated.

column111: Range across 5 trials under one-shot prompting; one-shot prompting reduced the initial mismatch count in all five trials compared with zero-shot.
column116: All 1278 variables are binary in the reference formulation for the equipment selection and layout planning problem (Mode A).
column121: Constraints in the complete reference formulation used in Mode A.
column126: Mode A trials, all using the same problem setting; differences among trials came only from variations in the LLM-generated formulations.
column128: The only quantitative outcome figures are the constraint-mismatch counts from the zero-shot vs one-shot comparison (Section 5.1: 'the number of mismatched constraints ranged from 179 to 417' under zero-shot and '39-59' under one-shot; Fig. 2). Problem-scale figures (1278 binary variables, 1362 constraints) come from Section 2/Table 1/Table 2, and candidate set sizes (10 robot arms, 8 grippers, 10 workpieces, 125 installation points of which 22 valid, 9 placement slots) are setup parameters in Table 2 rather than outcome metrics. No solver runtime, LLM cost/latency/token usage, or numeric success rates are reported; Mode B results (executable vs non-executable pick-and-place cases) are described only qualitatively (Section 6).
column130: All experiments - LLM formulation generation via the Gurobi Portal, constraint-level verification, Gurobi solving, and ROS 2 simulation - were designed, run, and judged by the authors on their own local setup (Sections 4.1, Table 2). No third-party testers, external experts, or participants other than the authors are mentioned anywhere in the paper.

For Mode B, Section 6 says 'representative optimization outputs were mapped to the ROS 2 / MoveIt Task Constructor environment', but the number of outputs/cases is not specified in the provided text.

column137: Repeated runs: 5 trials per prompting condition on the same problem (Table 2 'Number of trials: 5'; Fig. 2 shows trials 1-5 for both zero-shot and one-shot). llm_as_judge: false - outputs are verified by an LP constraint comparison tool and ROS 2/MoveIt simulation, not scored by an LLM (Sections 3, 4.1). efficiency_metrics_reported: 'no' - no LLM cost, latency, or token-usage figures appear; Table 2 lists only local hardware (AMD Ryzen 5 7530U, integrated GPU, 7 GiB RAM) and notes server-side LLM hardware specs were unavailable to the authors. statistical_testing: false - the zero-shot vs one-shot comparison (Section 5.1) reports ranges over 5 trials with no significance test or confidence interval.
column138: ["Prompt design alone is not sufficient: even with one-shot prompting, 39-59 constraint mismatches remained, so constraint-level verification and self-correction are still required (Sections 1, 5.1).", "Reference formulations are usually unavailable for realistic layout-planning problems, and preparing a complete reference formulation may require substantial expert effort whenever equipment candidates, layout conditions, or task requirements change (Section 1).", "The framework has not yet been extended to larger MIP problems, compared across multiple LLMs (formulation quality/stability may depend on the specific model), validated in real production environments or with a real robot, and the correction process needs more structured feedback for stability (Section 6)."]
column139: Author-stated limitations appear in Sections 1, 5.1, and 6: (i) 'prompt design alone does not guarantee correctness' and 'mismatches remained after one-shot generation' (Sections 1, 5.1); (ii) reference formulations and solutions are usually unavailable in realistic layout planning and are costly to prepare (Section 1); (iii) future-work items in Section 6 (larger MIP problems, multi-LLM comparison, more structured feedback, real-production and real-robot validation) implicitly mark the current scope limits.
column140: In Mode A, one-shot prompting reduced the initial constraint-mismatch count in all five trials relative to zero-shot prompting (zero-shot: 179-417 mismatched constraints; one-shot: 39-59) when LLM-generated Gurobi-compatible .lp files were compared constraint-by-constraint against a reference formulation, indicating that example-based prompting stabilizes variable naming and constraint structure but does not eliminate errors. Detected discrepancies are returned to the LLM as structured discrepancy reports for iterative self-correction. In Mode B (no reference formulation), representative optimization outputs were mapped to a ROS 2/MoveIt Task Constructor simulation, where both physically executable and non-executable pick-and-place solutions were identified through task-level validation of reachability, collision avoidance, safety distance, and motion feasibility.
column143: No human acts on intermediate or final LLM output inside the workflow. The human only supplies the initial specification: 'the human user provides the candidate sets, design conditions, and constraint categories, but does not manually write the complete formulation' (Sect. 3.1). The correction loop is fully automated, not human: 'detected discrepancies are returned to the LLM for self-correction' (Abstract) and 'the results are returned to the LLM through an API so that the formulation can be revised iteratively' (Sect. 6). Fig. 1 ends with 'If all checks are satisfied: The solution is considered deployable in a real production environment. Accept output (Verified formulation)' with no human review, approval, editing, or steering step described anywhere. Per schema, issuing the initial query does not count.
column149: Domain knowledge is encoded in explicit, machine-readable models that the system uses. The planning domain is specified as a complete MIP reference formulation: 'The complete reference formulation used in Mode A contains 1278 binary variables and 1362 constraints' (Sect. 2), with decision variables and constraints detailed in Table 1/Sect. 2, serialized in 'a solver-compatible .lp file format' (Sect. 3.3), used for constraint-level comparison (Mode A) and solved by Gurobi. The physical task domain is additionally encoded in a ROS2/MoveIt simulation used for validation: 'the obtained solution is evaluated in a Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2)-based simulation environment using MoveIt Task Constructor to check physical executability through pick-and-place task validation' (Abstract).
column151: mathematical-model applies twice: (1) the optimization model of the planning domain — binary selection/assignment variables (Table 1), a weighted cost-minimization objective, and selection, payload, gripper-opening, gripping-force, assignment and reachability constraints (Sect. 2) in Gurobi-compatible .lp format, used for solving and constraint-level verification; (2) the ROS 2 (Humble)/MoveIt Task Constructor simulation model of the pick-and-place domain (collision, reachability/workspace, motion feasibility) used for Mode B validation (Sect. 3, Sect. 4.1). No ontology, knowledge graph, standards encoding, relational database, or non-graph schema is described. The example formulations given in one-shot prompting (Sect. 3.2, Sect. 5.1) are few-shot prompt examples, which per schema do not count as domain knowledge formalization.
column152: The equipment selection and layout planning domain is formalized as a linear MIP model with 1278 binary decision variables (X_r, X_h, X_w for robot arm/gripper/workpiece selection; Y for installation-point selection; Z_{i,j} for placement-slot assignment) and 1362 constraints (single-selection, gripper opening width vs. workpiece diameter, robot/gripper payload, gripping force, candidate-point validity, assignment, reachability), with a weighted equipment-cost minimization objective, serialized in Gurobi-compatible .lp format (Sect. 2, Table 1). This reference model drives constraint-level comparison and self-correction in Mode A, while LLM-generated .lp models are solved by the Gurobi Optimizer. For Mode B, a ROS 2 Humble / MoveIt Task Constructor simulation environment encodes the physical pick-and-place task domain (collision check, reachability/workspace constraints, motion feasibility) and validates solutions when no reference formulation is available.
column155: Sect. 4.3 defines an explicit, repeatable protocol with stated metrics and procedure: '(i) the effect of prompting strategy, measured by the initial mismatch count under zero-shot and one-shot prompting; (ii) error detectability in Mode A, evaluated by mismatch counts and diagnostic categories; (iii) correction effectiveness, measured by the reduction in mismatches after feedback-based regeneration; and (iv) Mode B validation, evaluated by task-level simulation results and failure reasons.' Table 2 fixes the test items and conditions (5 trials, same problem setting, 10 robot-arm / 8 gripper / 10 workpiece candidates, 125 installation points, 9 placement slots, 1278 variables, 1362 constraints), and Sect. 5.1 reports the executed procedure and results (zero-shot 179–417 vs. one-shot 39–59 mismatched constraints across the five trials, Fig. 2).
column157: custom-test-set: the problem instance and scenarios were built by the authors ('we evaluate multiple scenarios with different levels of complexity by varying the number of candidates and the combinations of constraints', Sect. 4.1; Table 2). expert-ground-truth: generated formulations are scored against a manually prepared expert reference formulation ('the generated solver-compatible .lp file were compared with a reference formulation using constraint-level verification, and the number of mismatched constraints was counted', Sect. 5.1; 'the reference formulation is used only as a controlled benchmark for evaluating constraint-level verification and self-correction', Sect. 1). domain-specific-metric: constraint mismatch counts, diagnostic error categories, and task-level pick-and-place executability/failure reasons are task-specific metrics, not generic accuracy/F1 (Sect. 4.3). column158: Five trials of the same equipment-selection/layout-planning problem (10 robot arms, 8 grippers, 10 workpieces, 125 installation candidate points of which 22 valid, 9 placement slots; reference model with 1278 binary variables and 1362 constraints) were run in Mode A using Gurobot via the Gurobi Portal chat interface, with Gurobi as solver. Metrics: (i) initial constraint-mismatch count against the reference formulation under zero-shot vs. one-shot prompting (zero-shot: 179–417; one-shot: 39–59; Fig. 2); (ii) mismatch counts and diagnostic categories for error detectability; (iii) reduction in mismatches after feedback-based regeneration; (iv) Mode B task-level ROS2/MoveIt simulation results (executable vs. non-executable pick-and-place) with failure reasons.
column166: information-analysis: the LLM interprets the natural-language specification and generates the optimization model ('From this input, the LLM is expected to generate decision variables for equipment selection and layout assignment, an objective function for cost minimization, and constraints', Sect. 3.1), and the LP Constraint Comparison Tool analyzes the generated formulation ('Identify missing / extra / inconsistent constraints', Fig. 1). decision-selection: the solver driven by the LLM-generated model evaluates alternatives and chooses the final option ('The LP is then solved by an optimization solver to obtain a candidate solution, including selected equipment, a robot installation location, and a workpiece placement location', Sect. 3.3). action-implementation: the system writes the selected solution into the ROS2/MoveIt simulation and carries out the pick-and-place task ('Apply the solution to ROS 2-based simulation ... column168: The system selects and presents a single preferred option: Gurobi solves the generated MIP and outputs one candidate solution (selected equipment, robot installation location, workpiece placement; Sect. 3.3), which the framework automatically verifies and self-corrects, ending in 'If all checks are satisfied: The solution is considered deployable in a real production environment' (Fig. 1). column170: Architecture and setup are described in considerable detail: §3/Fig. 1 give the Mode A/Mode B workflow; §4.1 lists components ('LLM generator: Gurobot is used to generate solver-compatible .lp files', 'Optimization solver: The generated solver-compatible .lp files are solved with Gurobi', ROS 2-based simulation); §2/Table 1 specify the problem structure ('The complete reference formulation used in Mode A contains 1278 binary variables and 1362 constraints'); Table 2 gives OS, CPU, GPU, memory, and ROS version. column172: Study-type category A (implemented-validated): the framework was implemented (Gurobot + Gurobi + ROS 2/MoveIt Task Constructor, §4.1) and computational experiments were run. column174: Scope and failure modes are discussed in the main text: LLM formulations 'may include constraint-level errors, such as missing or redundant constraints, incorrect coefficients or indices, and wrong inequality directions' (Abstract); 'mismatches remained after one-shot generation, indicating that prompt design alone is not sufficient' (§5.1); the reference formulation 'is not assumed to be available in ordinary industrial use' (§1). [34]) is a general computer-science method, not a planning-domain framework.
column52: The paper introduces a modular framework for evaluating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on spatial tasks in production system planning (PSP). The framework connects a large-scale 3D production system scene (a USD-format model of a stud-welding station from an actual BMW Group body shop, rendered in Nvidia Omniverse) with VLM reasoning through five modules: VLM interface, render module, reasoning layer, camera control, and logging & metrics. Input: the VLM receives a Base64-encoded rendered image (downscaled to 2/3 resolution, 90% quality) of the 3D scene plus a natural-language planning question (e.g., verifying accessibility, counting robots, checking ram protection, localizing objects). Process: the VLM operates in a perception-reasoning-action loop (max 10 steps) - at each step it either returns a final answer or specifies camera translation/rotation deltas to actively change its viewpoint and gather more visual evidence. Output: a final answer to the spatial planning question, with a mandatory detailed justification for every decision. The framework enforces a strict Pydantic JSON output schema, stabilizes rendering before each capture (evidence control), and logs per-step images, performance data, and answers for combined qualitative (response/navigation correctness) and quantitative (number of steps, total translation/rotation, execution time) evaluation. The framework was validated with GPT-5.1 and Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct on four benchmark questions across scenes of varying complexity in an automotive planning scenario at the BMW Group.
column54: Only GPT-5.1 and Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct are deployed and evaluated with the paper's own framework (Section IV.A: 'We use one state-of-the-art model (GPT-5.1) and one open-access model (Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct)'; results in Table II). Other models mentioned are NOT coded in 'models' because they appear only in related work, discussion, or illustrative material: CosmosReason1 (Nvidia 56B VLM, Section II.B related work), MaViLa (Fan et al., Section II.B related work), GPT-4v and Claude-3.5 (SOTA models discussed for specific applications in Section II.B), LLaVA 1.6 34B (evaluated by Picard et al. in related work, Section II.B), SIMA-2 (DeepMind, Section II.A discussion), YOLO and DINO (non-LLM vision architecture comparisons, Section II.A), and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (shown only as an example configuration in the UI screenshot Fig. 2, Section III.B; no evaluation results are reported for it).
column55: Both GPT-5.1 (state-of-the-art, proprietary) and Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct (open-access) are run through the same framework on the same four benchmark questions (five repetitions each, 240 data points total) to validate the framework's functional correctness, reliability, and suitability; the authors explicitly state that a detailed model comparison is not the goal of the study (Section IV.A).

column67: No weight updates are applied anywhere in the method. column71: zero-shot: models are applied without in-context examples; the paper explicitly highlights 'flexible adaptation to various planning tasks through zero-shot inference' (Section I) and the framework provides no worked examples. structured-output: 'the output follows a strict Pydantic schema' that 'automatically enforces structural and semantic constraints on model outputs' (Section III.D), and the VLM interface 'parses the response from the structured JSON output' (Section III.B). ReAct: Algorithm 1 (Section III.A) defines a perception-reasoning-action loop in which the VLM interleaves reasoning with tool actions - at each step it either emits a camera action (translation/rotation delta) or a final answer, and 'the model must provide a detailed explanation for every decision' (Section III.D) - which is structurally the ReAct pattern of interleaved reasoning and acting. Note: the claim-control explanation requirement has CoT-like elements, but it is realized inside this ReAct-style loop rather than as a separate CoT technique, so CoT is not coded separately.
column74: single-agent: One VLM agent loops over reasoning and tool use. The VLM's policy maps the interaction history, question, and current observation to either a subsequent camera action or a final answer (Section III.A, Algorithm 1), i.e., it decides its next step at run time. The five modules (VLM interface, render module, reasoning layer, camera control, logging & metrics; Section III.B, Fig. 1) are deterministic support components around this one agent. There is no supervisor agent, no peer agents, and no developer-fixed sequence of multiple specialised LLM roles, so multi-agent, supervisor-agent, and pipeline do not apply.
column76: none: The method is a single autonomous VLM agent in a perception-reasoning-action loop. Per the schema definition, 'none' applies to 'a single call, or a single autonomous agent, also when deterministic code validates, repairs or scores its output and feeds back in a loop'. The render, camera-control, and logging modules are deterministic code supporting the single agent; there are no LLM calls with distinct roles (no prompt-chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, or evaluator-optimizer patterns) anywhere in the method (Sections III.A-III.B).
column80: agent_memory = short-term: within each task run the VLM receives the full interaction history Ht = {(o0, a0), ..., (ot-1, at-1), ot} (Section III.A), and the reasoning layer 'receives the question and the interaction history as input' (Section III.B); the paper describes 'minimal memory and state handling' (Section III.B). No persistent memory across tasks/sessions is reported, so long-term does not apply. planning_reflection = false: no explicit self-critique or reflection mechanism (e.g., plan-and-execute, Reflexion) is described; the VLM reasons about the next action from history but does not critique or reflect on its own prior outputs in a structured step. tool_use = true: the VLM itself decides at run time whether to output camera translation/rotation deltas (which invoke the camera-control module to change the viewpoint) or a final answer (Algorithm 1, Section III.A) - run-time function/action invocation decided by the LLM.

column84: The proposed method is an evaluation/benchmarking framework for Vision-Language Models on spatial Visual Question Answering tasks in production system planning (§I, §III). It formalizes the problem as VQA with a perception-reasoning-action loop (§III.A, Algorithm 1), in which the VLM iteratively adjusts virtual camera viewpoints to gather evidence and answer questions about 3D production scenes. This is not an optimization/OR problem: there is no objective function, constraint set, or solution search performed by the method. The logged metrics (response/navigation correctness, steps, translation, rotation, execution time; Table I, §III.C) are recorded for evaluation, not optimized by the framework. Optimization-related mentions such as RL training of CosmosReason1 and RAG in MaViLa appear only in related work (§II.B), not in the proposed method.
column86: 'none' because optimization_tradition_present is false. The method's own formalization (§III.A) is a VQA problem statement with a sequential camera-navigation and answering loop, not a mathematical program, an explicit objective/constraint search, or an MCDM scoring procedure.
column88: Empty set because the method itself uses no optimization paradigm. The framework consists of a VLM interface, 3D renderer (Nvidia Omniverse), reasoning layer with API integrations, camera control via affine coordinate transformations, and a logging/metrics module (§III.B, Fig. 1). column91: 'none' (exclusive) because there is no optimizer in the method for the LLM/VLM to interact with. The VLM's iterative viewpoint adjustment is a perception-reasoning loop for question answering, which per the schema does not count as optimization.
column93: No optimization solver is used or mentioned anywhere in the paper. The framework's technical stack involves VLM inference APIs, 3D rendering, and metric logging (§III.B), so 'NR' applies.
column96: The paper validates its evaluation framework by scoring VLM responses on an author-built benchmark: four questions randomly selected from the benchmarking dataset are applied to 3D production scenes of varying complexity, and each run receives a binary correct/incorrect score against expected answers (Section IV.A; results in Table II, Section IV.B). The test items come from a single real case (BMW Group body shop scenario), but the evaluation mechanism is a benchmark test rather than a case worked through end-to-end; no user study, field deployment, or controlled comparison of method variants is present (the two VLMs are evaluation subjects/backbones, not conditions of the paper's own method).
column98: The validation was conducted within a real automotive planning scenario at the BMW Group (Abstract; Section IV.A): the core data is a 3D scene of an actual BMW body shop stud-welding station - the organisation's own production-system planning data (Section III.C) - and the benchmark questions were collected from BMW planning experts, reflecting 'realistic challenges that planners typically address in their daily work' (Section III.C). Per the schema criteria, real core data with researcher execution and expert-constructed questions does not make the episode artificial. Note (?): the run itself is a controlled, test-set-style session (fixed camera start, default sampling parameters, max 10 steps; Section IV.A), which under the coarse FEDS shorthand ('test set = artificial') could be coded artificial; coded naturalistic because the core data, organisation, and problem are real.

column138: ["The framework's navigation accuracy is limited: VLMs move in larger steps than humans and, once a move is wrong, quickly lose orientation and cannot easily recover; more continuous image capturing could help, but most VLMs currently lack the processing speed and bandwidth to handle such high image throughput (Section IV.B).", "The framework currently relies on visual input only; the authors propose combining visual input with scene-graph metadata (object names and coordinates) so the model can use numeric and symbolic information when visual cues are unclear (Section IV.B).", "Both evaluated VLMs showed limitations in spatial navigation, especially in scenes requiring more complex camera movement; overall, the results indicate VLMs are still far from autonomously navigating large 3D production system scenes and performing all validation tasks (Section IV.B).", "The framework's human-mirroring design - first-person navigation with conventional rendering software - ensures comparability with human planners but may constrain AI to the same perceptual limits that define human planning (Section V)."]
column139: Section IV.B ('The validation results also revealed several areas where the framework itself can be improved') states the navigation-accuracy limitation, the VLM bandwidth constraint on continuous image capture, and the missing scene-graph metadata integration, and concludes that VLMs are 'still far from being able to autonomously navigate' large 3D production scenes. Section V adds the reflection that the human-mirroring first-person design 'may also constrain AI to the same perceptual limits that define human planning.'
column140: Validation with two representative VLMs (GPT-5.1, state-of-the-art; Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct, open-access) confirmed the framework's functional correctness and flexibility: the VLM interface, scene rendering, camera control, reasoning layer, and logging operated reliably, and models could be exchanged within seconds (Section IV.B). Across four benchmark questions (five runs per model), GPT-5.1 achieved higher average response correctness than Qwen3 (0.40 vs. 0.25); both handled fixed-viewpoint reasoning but failed on navigation-requiring questions (both scored 0.00 on Q3), with navigation correctness averaging 0.70 (GPT-5.1) vs. 0.65 (Qwen3) and average execution times of 18.95 s vs. 23.02 s. The authors conclude that VLMs cannot yet autonomously navigate large 3D production scenes or perform validation tasks overnight, but that the framework provides a practical, reproducible foundation for benchmarking VLM progress toward industrial readiness.
column143: Section III.C states the framework adopts 'combining human (qualitative) and automatic (quantitative) evaluation' (Picard et al. methodology), and Table I lists qualitative metrics (response correctness Y/N, navigation correctness Y/N) that require human judgment of the VLM's final output. Section IV.A describes the procedure: 'For each run, a binary score of 1 is assigned when the answer is correct and 0 when it is not.' Human evaluators thus review the final VLM output (answer and navigation behavior) inside the evaluation framework's workflow, exceeding the schema's exclusion of merely issuing the initial query or reading the final answer. Uncertainty (?): the human step is post-run scoring for benchmarking rather than an operational intervention that steers the VLM; no standard HITL pattern fits, hence 'other'.
column145: The human role is post-run qualitative evaluation/scoring of final VLM outputs (response correctness, navigation correctness; Table I, Sections III.C and IV.A). It does not match approval-gate (no correction/gating before the workflow proceeds), iterative-feedback (no guidance steering the next iteration; the five repetitions per question are independent), escalation-protocol (the system does not request human input), human-override (no editing/vetoing of intermediate decisions), or what-if-interface (no scenario exploration by changing inputs). Coded as 'other': human expert review/scoring of final outputs within the evaluation workflow.
column146: The framework combines human (qualitative) and automatic (quantitative) evaluation following Picard et al. After each VLM run, human evaluators review the logged answer and navigation behavior and assign binary scores for response correctness and navigation correctness to assess reasoning validity; quantitative metrics (number of steps, total translation, total rotation, execution time) are captured automatically.
column147: Human experts/researchers qualitatively evaluate VLM outputs (response correctness, navigation correctness) by reviewing logged answers and navigation behavior and assigning binary scores after each run, as part of the framework's combined human-automatic evaluation methodology.
column149: No explicit, reusable, machine-readable domain knowledge structure is used by the system. The VLM reasons from rendered images and natural-language questions. The 3D scene is stored in USD format but serves as rendering input, not as knowledge for reasoning; the paper explicitly identifies combining visual input with scene-graph metadata as a future improvement (Section IV.B: 'A second improvement would be to combine the visual input with existing metadata, such as object names and coordinates stored in a scene graph'), confirming such structured knowledge is not currently used. The Pydantic schema (Section III.D) enforces a response output contract (answer/explanation/camera-action structure) but does not encode production-planning domain knowledge. Prompt background information and scale hints are free text, which per the schema does not count.
column155: The paper defines an explicit, repeatable evaluation protocol with defined test items, metrics, and procedure. Test items: four benchmark questions applied to 3D production scenes of varying complexity (Section IV.A, Fig. 4). Metrics: qualitative (response correctness, navigation correctness) and quantitative (number of steps, total translation, total rotation, execution time) per Table I. Procedure: 'Each experiment is repeated five times per model and question... The starting position of the virtual camera is fixed... the maximum number of reasoning steps is set to ten. All sampling parameters, such as temperature and top-k, remain unchanged... In total, 240 data points are obtained' (Section IV.A).
column157: custom-test-set: The benchmark dataset and sample questions were built by the authors for this paper ('The provided sample questions were collected from planning experts at the BMW Group', Section III.C) and the 3D scene (BMW body-shop stud-welding station) was constructed for evaluation; it is not a reused public benchmark. expert-ground-truth: VLM outputs are scored against correct answers reflecting expert planning knowledge; questions were collected from planning experts and include planning-judgment tasks (e.g., 'Would another robot fit within this cell?', 'Can the worker access the control cabinets?', Fig. 4), and the methodology combines human (qualitative) evaluation (Section III.C). Binary correct/incorrect scoring is used rather than a graded rubric, and the efficiency metrics (steps, translation, rotation, time) are framework navigation measures rather than planning-domain metrics such as throughput or cost.
column158: The framework evaluates VLMs on spatial tasks in production system planning using a benchmark of expert-collected questions applied to a 3D scene of a BMW Group body-shop stud-welding station (USD format). Validation used four questions (two solvable from a fixed viewpoint, two requiring navigation) with two VLMs (GPT-5.1, Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct), five repetitions per model/question, fixed starting camera position, max ten reasoning steps, and default sampling parameters (240 data points). Scoring combines human qualitative evaluation (binary response/navigation correctness) with automatic quantitative metrics (steps, total translation in cm, total rotation in degrees, execution time in seconds).
column166: information-acquisition: The VLM actively gathers visual observations at run time by controlling a virtual camera ('simulated sensor') in the 3D production scene ('The use of VLMs not only to interpret rendered images but also to actively specify camera states represents a novel approach', Section III.A; 'This camera acts as a simulated sensor and enables first-person exploration of the 3D production scene', Section III.B). The VLM iteratively applies camera deltas to collect evidence beyond the initially given viewpoint, constituting dynamic, need-driven information gathering rather than deterministic pre-processing. information-analysis: The VLM integrates and interprets visual observations and interaction history to reason about geometric relations and produce answers to spatial planning questions (e.g., accessibility, object localization; 'The VLM's reasoning maps the interaction history, the query, and the observation to either a subsequent action or a final answer', Section III.A). The system does not perform decision-selection (it does not evaluate/rank planning alternatives) or action-implementation (it returns answers; it does not write decisions into plans or systems). Uncertainty (?): observations are rendered images of the given 3D scene; the schema's exclusion of 'rendered images' as encoding could be read to exclude this stage, but the VLM-driven dynamic viewpoint selection constitutes active sensor querying rather than passive encoding.
column168: The VLM produces candidate answers/assessments to spatial planning questions (e.g., 'Would another robot fit within this cell?', 'Can the worker access the control cabinets?', Fig. 4), which human planners evaluate and use to make the final planning decisions. The system does not select, rank, or recommend specific planning options (no 2-recommendation), nor does it decide or implement any planning action (no 3-veto/4-autonomous). Coded as 1-options: the system generates outputs for humans to evaluate and decide, though strictly the VLM generates question answers/assessments rather than explicit planning options.

column18: The paper proposes the Parser-Coder-Validator (PCV) prompting framework and validates it in an artificial/lab setting: a controlled benchmark comparison of four LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok-Code-Fast-1) on 687 optimization problems derived from the public OptiGuide repository across three domains (Coffee Supply Chain, Facility Location, Workforce Scheduling), with a defined accuracy metric (Abstract; Sections III.C–III.E; Tables II–III). There is no evaluation in operational practice—no real organization, real users, or real company data in operational use; the instances are public benchmark problems—so per the Wieringa facet this is validation-research rather than evaluation-research. The thorough multi-model, multi-domain evaluation with defined metrics also rules out solution-proposal.
column20: PCV was implemented and run end-to-end: the framework is described as 'Sequential role-based prompting (3 API calls to same LLM)' with data passed between stages (Fig. 1, Section III.B), and quantitative results are reported for both the LLMFP baseline (Table II) and PCV (Table III) across all four models and three domains (e.g., PCV accuracy up to 96.4% in Workforce Scheduling, 95.8% in Facility Location). The evaluation protocol and metric are explicitly defined in Section III.E: 'Performance is measured by accuracy: the proportion of questions for which the model's final parsed answer matches the ground-truth optimal value.' Working system + controlled evaluation under a defined protocol with defined metrics → implemented-validated.
column22: No industry sector is reported for the study. The work is academic research conducted at Al Akhawayn University in Ifrane, Morocco (author affiliations), and the evaluation uses public benchmark problems from the OptiGuide repository (Section III.D: 'derived from the publicly available OptiGuide repository (github.com/microsoft/OptiGuide)'). Although the problem scenarios model supply chain, facility placement, and workforce rostering settings, the paper does not situate the research within any specific industry sector, so NR.
column23: LLM-based combinatorial optimization, evaluated on three benchmark domains: Coffee Supply Chain (multi-stage capacitated network flow), Facility Location (Capacitated Facility Location Problem), and Workforce Scheduling (employee rostering)
column24: Section III.D and Table I ('Benchmark Domains') report the evaluation benchmark of 687 optimization problems across three domains derived from the publicly available OptiGuide repository: Coffee Supply Chain (273 questions, multi-stage production optimization with continuous variables), Facility Location (165 questions, Capacitated Facility Location Problem with binary decision variables), and Workforce Scheduling (249 questions, employee rostering with time-based constraints).
column25: Can modular prompting architectures that incorporate validated, machine-verifiable intermediate representations consistently enhance LLM-based optimization across diverse models?
column26: Section II.B states the research question verbatim: 'This gap motivates our research question: Can modular prompting architectures that incorporate validated, machine-verifiable intermediate representations consistently enhance LLM-based optimization across diverse models?' The paper addresses it by proposing PCV and conducting 'a comprehensive comparison with LLMFP across four state-of-the-art LLMs on 687 optimization problems, allowing us to separate the contributions of architectural design from those of model choice' (Section II.B). No other research questions are formally enumerated.
column28: Mapped from the three benchmark domains (§III.D, Table I). (1) Facility Location (165 problems): described as 'Strategic facility placement (Capacitated Facility Location Problem) with binary decision variables' involving 5 plants and 4 warehouses with plant open/close decisions -> site-selection (facility location/site selection). (2) Coffee Supply Chain (273 problems): a 'multi-stage capacitated network flow problem' sourcing from 3 suppliers, roasting at 2 roasteries, and distributing two product types to 3 cafes -> SC-network-design as the closest vocabulary fit for a multi-echelon supply chain network problem. Boundary case (?): the coffee questions optimize flows on a fixed network (allocation) rather than structurally designing the network, so this mapping is loose. (3) Workforce Scheduling (249 problems): employee rostering is operational personnel scheduling that fits no subdomain in the closed vocabulary; noted as out-of-vocabulary rather than force-mapped.
column30: Workforce/employee shift scheduling (rostering): assignment of 7 workers to shifts over 14 days minimizing total payroll cost subject to worker availability, daily shift coverage requirements, weekly workload limits and conflict rules (§III.D).
column31: (1) facility-location: the Facility Location domain is a Capacitated Facility Location Problem whose binary variables encode plant open/close decisions (§III.D, Table I). (2) SC-network-configuration: the Coffee Supply Chain domain is a multi-echelon problem across suppliers, roasteries (plants) and distribution to cafes (§III.D); closest available category, though the questions allocate flows on a fixed network rather than configure its structure (?). (3) other: Workforce Scheduling (employee shift rostering, §III.D) is a core benchmark task (249 of 687 problems, and the domain of LLMFP's headline 95% accuracy) not covered by any standard category. No requirements-elicitation, layout, simulation, make-or-buy or investment tasks are performed.
column33: Coffee Supply Chain spans three processes: sourcing beans from 3 suppliers (procurement), roasting at 2 roasteries (production), and distributing two product types to 3 cafes (distribution) - §III.D. Facility Location concerns 5 plants (production) and 4 warehouses with transportation to satisfy demand (distribution) - §III.D. Workforce Scheduling (employee rostering, §III.D) concerns staffing of operations and is loosely mapped to production (?; the SCP Matrix has no dedicated personnel process). Sales is not addressed: demand appears only as a fixed constraint/parameter, not as a decision.

The only temporal parameter is the rostering window in Workforce Scheduling - 'An employee rostering assignment problem involving 7 workers and 14 days' (§III.D) - which is a problem-instance parameter (parallel to '5 plants and 4 warehouses') rather than an author-stated planning horizon; Coffee Supply Chain and Facility Location state no horizon. ? Boundary note: if the 14-day rostering period were counted as an explicit horizon, the answer would be Y with value '14 days'.

Strategic: Facility Location - 'Binary variables encode plant open/close decisions' (§III.D) determine which plants exist/open, a system-configuring decision (system_configuring_decision = true), so Strategic is selected per rule. Tactical: Coffee Supply Chain - allocation of shipping/roasting flows across the existing fixed network (3 suppliers, 2 roasteries, 3 cafes) under capacity and demand constraints (§III.D), i.e., mid-term allocation of existing resources (? judged tactical rather than operational given the capacitated network-flow planning nature). Operational: Workforce Scheduling - short-term shift rostering over a 14-day window ('7 workers and 14 days', §III.D).
column42: Table I (§III.D) explicitly labels the Facility Location domain 'Strategic facility placement (Capacitated Facility Location Problem) with binary decision variables' - the 'strategic' label is applied to the facility placement decision that the method supports. No 'tactical' or 'operational' label is applied to any decision elsewhere; e.g., 'three strategic reasons' (§III.A, motivation for choosing Z3) is not a planning-tier claim.
column44: The Facility Location decision determines which plants exist/open in the network: 'The Facility Location domain (165 questions) instantiates a Capacitated Facility Location Problem (CFLP) involving 5 plants and 4 warehouses. Binary variables encode plant open/close decisions.' (§III.D). Open/close decisions create or remove facilities (sites), determining what exists in the system; scenario constraints confirm this, e.g., 'close_plant' -> solver.add(open[plant_id] == 0) and 'force_open_plant' -> solver.add(open[plant_id] == 1) (Fig. 3, §III.B). The other domains are not system-configuring: Coffee Supply Chain allocates flows on a fixed network; Workforce Scheduling assigns shifts to a fixed workforce.

column47: Determines which of 5 plants are open (binary open/close decision variables) in a capacitated network serving 4 warehouses; the objective minimizes total fixed opening costs plus variable transportation costs subject to demand satisfaction, plant capacity, and linking constraints (§III.D). Benchmark questions include scenarios forcing plants open or closed (e.g., 'close_plant', 'force_open_plant'; Fig. 3).
column49: No planning-domain reference model structures the paper's scope: VDI 5200, the Supply Chain Planning Matrix, Lanza et al. (2019), Wiendahl-Nyhuis and Melo-Nickel-Saldanha-da-Gama (2009) are neither cited nor used. The paper's organizing frameworks are LLM prompting architectures - the LLMFP baseline (Hao et al. [1]) and the proposed PCV framework - plus the Z3 SMT solver [2], with benchmark domains taken from the OptiGuide repository [15]. Background citations (chain-of-thought [8], tree-of-thoughts [11], self-consistency [10], Self-Refine [14], OPRO [4]) are general prompting/optimization methods, which per the schema do not count.
column50: The study compares LLM prompting architectures (LLMFP vs. PCV) on combinatorial optimization benchmarks; it uses no planning-domain framework to define or structure its planning scope. Its scope is instead defined by the three OptiGuide benchmark domains (Coffee Supply Chain, Facility Location, Workforce Scheduling) and the LLMFP/PCV prompting pipelines built on the Z3 solver.
column52: The LLM's role is shifted from solver to translator: it converts natural-language combinatorial optimization problems (question + domain context + optimization requirements) into formal, executable Python code built on the Z3 SMT solver, which computes the optimal solution. The paper's Parser-Coder-Validator (PCV) framework decomposes this translation into three specialized stages: (1) Parser — semantic extraction of entities, constraints, parameters and the optimization objective into a structured JSON schema serving as a contract between user intent and solver execution; (2) Coder — transformation of the JSON specification into executable Z3 Python code with constraint-handling templates (e.g., binary open/close variables, UNSAT handling); (3) Validator — pre-execution static analysis checking constraint completeness, type safety and UNSAT robustness, returning a structured JSON error report that triggers regeneration of the Coder step. Generated code is executed in a secure environment and the parsed numerical answer is compared against the ground-truth optimal value. PCV is compared with the monolithic LLMFP baseline (single-pass script generation with self-assessment iterating up to five times) on 687 problems across Coffee Supply Chain, Facility Location and Workforce Scheduling domains, yielding decision-support guidance on model-framework pairing.

column71: structured-output: the PCV Parser stage constrains output to a 'structured JSON schema' specification, the Coder consumes it under valid templates, and the Validator returns a 'structured error report (JSON)' (Sections I, III.B; 'structured JSON enforcement', Section IV.B). other (role prompting): Fig. 1 explicitly labels the approach 'Sequential role-based prompting (3 API calls to same LLM)' with specialized Parser/Coder/Validator roles. column72: Sequential role-based prompting: three role-specialized API calls (Parser, Coder, Validator) to the same LLM, with the framework passing data between stages (Fig. 1).
column74: The paper's PCV framework is a fixed, developer-defined sequence of three specialized LLM roles — Parser, Coder, Validator — with the framework, not the LLM, controlling the flow ('Sequential role-based prompting (3 API calls to same LLM). Framework passes data between stages', Fig. 1; Section III.B). No LLM component decides its next action or tool call at run time, so per the schema this is a pipeline rather than an agent architecture. The LLMFP baseline is likewise a monolithic single-pass script generation with a developer-fixed self-assessment loop (up to five iterations, Section III.A).
column76: prompt-chaining: the Parser LLM call produces a JSON specification that is consumed by the Coder LLM call, whose generated code is then checked by the Validator LLM call — a fixed sequence in which each call processes the previous output (Fig. 1; Section III.B). evaluator-optimizer: the Coder (generator) LLM call produces Z3 code and the Validator (evaluator) LLM call critiques it, returning a structured JSON error report that 'triggers a regeneration of the Coder step' (Section III.B) — an LLM-to-LLM feedback loop (not feedback from deterministic code), so both patterns are coded per 0.10.4. The LLMFP baseline additionally contains a self-assessment loop in which the model critiques its own answer and iterates up to five times (Section III.A). No routing, parallelization or orchestrator-workers patterns are present.
column80: agent_memory = short-term: within one problem-solving task the framework passes the structured JSON specification, generated code and error reports between the three LLM calls ('Framework passes data between stages', Fig. 1), and the LLMFP baseline iterates up to five times with self-assessment (Section III.A) — working memory within a task/session; no persistent memory across the 687 problems is described. planning_reflection = true: LLMFP includes an explicit self-assessment stage ('the model performs a self-assessment to determine whether the answer satisfies the user's original request', Section III.A), and PCV's Validator LLM call critiques the Coder's generated code before execution, feeding back a structured error report that triggers regeneration (Section III.B). tool_use = false: the LLM does not itself decide to call tools/functions at run time; code execution and Z3 solver invocation are developer-fixed pipeline steps (coded under integrations).
column82: solver: the execution backend relies on the Z3 Theorem Prover, 'a high-performance Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver' (Section III.A); the LLM translates problems into Z3-based Python code whose solution is computed by Z3. code-execution: the generated Python script is executed in a secure environment and its raw output returned for interpretation (Section III.A).
