column84: True. The proposed Parser-Coder-Validator (PCV) framework (like the LLMFP baseline it improves) itself formulates and solves combinatorial optimization problems: the LLM translates natural-language problem descriptions into executable Z3 solver code, which the system executes to compute solutions (§I: 'converts the natural language problems into executable Python code utilizing the Z3 solver'; §III.A, §III.B). The 687 benchmark problems are explicit optimization problems with decision variables, objectives, and constraints across three domains (§III.D, Table I), and the model's final parsed answer is scored against ground-truth optimal values (§III.E). This is an LLM-generated model that is then solved, so optimization is not merely background or a comparison baseline.
column86: High. The LLM-generated code constitutes an explicit mathematical program: decision variables (e.g., open = [Int(f'open_{i}')] for binary plant open/close decisions; binary worker-shift-day assignments; continuous variables in Coffee Supply Chain), constraints encoded via solver.add(...) (capacity, demand, flow-balance, linking, coverage), and objectives via solver.minimize(total_cost) under Optimize() (§III.B, Figs. 2-3). Z3 solves these exactly; a response is counted correct only if the numerical answer exactly equals the ground-truth optimal value (§III.E). Full domain models (variables, objectives, constraints) are specified in §III.D.
column88: Two paradigms are involved. (1) CP: the solving engine is the Z3 Theorem Prover, 'a high-performance Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver' (a SAT extension) invoked via the z3solver Python API with Optimize()/solver.check() (§III.A). (2) MILP-LP: the formulated problems are linear programs — Coffee Supply Chain is a multi-stage capacitated network flow problem with continuous variables; Facility Location is a Capacitated Facility Location Problem with binary decision variables; Workforce Scheduling uses binary worker-shift-day assignments — all with linear cost-minimization objectives and linear capacity/demand/flow/coverage constraints (§III.D, Table I; linear solver.add/solver.minimize in Figs. 2-3). The paper never uses the terms MILP/LP, but the linear mixed-integer structure is clearly demonstrated; Z3 solves these linear-arithmetic optimization problems via SMT.
column91: formulator: PCV's Parser translates the NL question + domain context into a structured JSON specification (entities, constraints, objective) and the Coder transforms it into executable Z3 Python code (§III.B, Figs. 1-3); LLMFP likewise has the LLM translate NL problems into Z3 code (§III.A). verifier: PCV's Validator is an LLM call acting as a static analyzer that checks completeness (all JSON constraints present in code), type safety (int vs real decision variables), constraint correctness, objective alignment, and robustness (UNSAT handling), returning a structured error report that triggers Coder regeneration (§III.B, Fig. 1) — model-correctness checks beyond mere syntax, so the syntax-check exclusion does not apply; LLMFP also includes a self-assessment step on the answer (§III.A). solver-orchestrator and result-interpreter: §III.A describes the pipeline in which the system executes the LLM-written Z3 code and 'returns the raw output, which the model interprets into a natural language answer' — per the 0.10.5 rule, LLM-written code invoking the solver with the output fed back to the LLM counts as solver-orchestrator even though the framework executes the code. ? Uncertainty: that paragraph opens 'The PCV pipeline proceeds through six stages' but sits in §III.A ('The LLMFP Paradigm') and conflicts with PCV's three-stage description (abstract, §III.B, Fig. 1), so it plausibly describes the LLMFP baseline (apparent typo); PCV's own description does not explicitly mention post-execution interpretation or solver-output feedback. These two roles are included per the literal text, with the attribution ambiguity flagged. direct-optimizer does not apply: the LLM never proposes solutions itself; Z3 computes them.
column93: Z3 Theorem Prover — 'a high-performance Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver developed by Microsoft Research', used through its Python API (z3solver) with Optimize() (§III.A). LLM-generated code invokes Z3 (solver.check(), solver.minimize(), solver.model()); Figs. 2-3 show the Z3 Python code. Z3 was chosen for expressiveness across integer/bit-vector/real theories, its MIT open-source license, and LLM code proficiency (§III.A).
column94: The method translates natural-language combinatorial optimization problems into Z3 solver code that is executed to compute optimal values. Benchmark problems (687, from the OptiGuide repository) span three domains: (1) Coffee Supply Chain — multi-stage capacitated network flow (3 suppliers, 2 roasteries, 3 cafes, 2 product types) with continuous variables; minimize total shipping and roasting cost subject to supplier capacity, roastery capacity, cafe demand, and flow-balance constraints. (2) Facility Location — Capacitated Facility Location Problem (5 plants, 4 warehouses) with binary plant open/close decision variables; minimize total fixed opening costs plus variable transportation costs subject to demand satisfaction, plant capacity, and linking constraints. (3) Workforce Scheduling — employee rostering (7 workers, 14 days) with binary worker-shift-day assignment variables; minimize total payroll cost subject to worker availability, daily shift coverage, weekly workload limits, and conflict rules. In PCV, the Parser outputs a JSON specification (task_type, constraints, entities) that the Coder compiles into Z3 Python code declaring Int/binary variables, adding constraints via solver.add(), setting the objective via solver.minimize() under Optimize(), and handling UNSAT results.
column96: The paper's own method (PCV) and the LLMFP baseline are evaluated on a fixed set of 687 optimization problems (273 Coffee Supply Chain, 165 Facility Location, 249 Workforce Scheduling) derived from the public OptiGuide repository, with each model's final parsed answer scored against ground-truth optimal values (§III.D, §III.E, Tables II–III) — a test-set design. The study is also explicitly a controlled comparison of two prompting conditions (PCV vs LLMFP) on the same tasks across four LLMs (§IV.A–§IV.B), which fits the quasi-experimental type 'controlled comparison of conditions or groups on the same tasks'.
column98: All evaluation episodes use benchmark optimization problems from the public OptiGuide repository, executed by the researchers via the OpenRouter API and scored automatically against ground-truth optimal values (§III.C–§III.E). No real users, real organizations, or real operational data are involved — the three domains (coffee supply chain, capacitated facility location, workforce rostering) are modeled benchmark scenarios. Per FEDS, a test-set/benchmark evaluation of this kind is artificial.

column139: There is no dedicated limitations section; author-stated limitations are scattered across the results discussion and conclusions. §IV.B reports the GPT-OSS-20B regression under PCV on Coffee Supply Chain (explicit parsing failing on subtle modifiers); §IV.C labels GPT-OSS-120B 'Ceiling-Constrained'; §V's future-work items (architectural modifications with larger models, hybrid neural-symbolic approaches, cross-lingual evaluation) imply current scope limitations. The monolithic-design weaknesses of LLMFP (error propagation, no intermediate validation, parsing difficulties; §I) describe the baseline method, not the paper's own contribution, so they are not coded as limitations of this work.
column140: Across 687 optimization problems from the OptiGuide repository in three domains, the authors first established LLMFP baselines for four LLMs: GPT-OSS-120B was strongest (82.65% Coffee, 90.30% Facility, 95.00% Workforce), while Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-OSS-20B and Grok-Code-Fast-1 fell below 45% on Facility Location; log analysis attributed most failures to formatting/parsing and syntax issues rather than reasoning errors. The proposed three-stage PCV framework (Parser–Coder–Validator) matched or outperformed LLMFP for nearly all model-domain combinations, with dramatic Facility Location gains (Gemini +57.02%, GPT-OSS-20B +52.09%, Grok +50.95%) and Grok improving 39.71% overall to reach the highest overall accuracy of any configuration (92.43%). PCV raised the performance floor — the worst PCV configuration (87.20%) exceeded the best non-frontier LLMFP configuration (67.63%) — although GPT-OSS-20B regressed 3.97% on Coffee Supply Chain. The authors conclude that framework design matters as much as model selection and provide deployment guidelines: Grok-PCV offers the best cost-effectiveness, while GPT-OSS-120B-LLMFP provides robust accuracy (89.32%) with minimal engineering overhead.
column143: No HITL pattern is described. The PCV pipeline is fully automated: Fig. 1 (Section III.B) shows 'Sequential role-based prompting (3 API calls to same LLM)' with the framework passing data between stages, and the Validator 'acts as a static analyzer' whose structured error reports trigger automated regeneration of the Coder step (Section III.B). The LLMFP baseline's loop is model self-assessment, not human feedback: 'the model performs a self-assessment to determine whether the answer satisfies the user's original request, iterating up to five times if necessary' (Section III.A). Evaluation scoring is likewise automated ('output in a format that the evaluation parser cannot extract', Section III.E). No human review, approval, editing, escalation, or steering of intermediate or final LLM output is mentioned anywhere in the paper.
column149: True. PCV encodes domain knowledge in explicit, machine-readable structures used at run time. Section III.B: the Parser Stage 'translates the natural language question and domain context into a structured JSON specification... extracting entities (suppliers, roasteries, cafes), constraints (capacity limits, demand requirements), and the optimization objective (minimize cost, maximize profit)', producing 'a structured JSON schema that serves as a contract between the user's intent and the solver's execution' that is validated and passed between stages. The Coder Stage transforms this JSON into executable Z3 Python code 'constraining generation to valid templates' (Section I), with explicit constraint-handling templates (Fig. 3), and the generated Z3 code specifies the optimization model (variables, constraints, objective) that the system executes (Fig. 2; Section III.A: 'The system then executes this code in a secure environment').
column151: structured-schema: the Parser outputs a structured JSON specification/schema of domain entities, constraints and objective that LLM output must conform to and that is passed between stages (Section III.B; Fig. 2 input example: task_type minimize, constraints [close_plant], entities {plant_id: 0}). code-template: the Coder Stage generates Z3 code 'constraining generation to valid templates' (Section I), with explicit constraint-handling code templates in Fig. 3 (e.g., IF 'close_plant' in constraints: Extract plant_id from entities. Add: solver.add(open[plant_id] == 0)). mathematical-model: the generated Z3 Python code implements the optimization model of the planning domain - decision variables, constraints and objective (Fig. 2: solver = Optimize(), solver.add(open[0] == 0), solver.minimize(total_cost)) - and is executed by the system via the Z3 solver (Section III.A). Per 0.10.5, model code implementing an optimization model is coded as both code-template and mathematical-model.
column152: PCV formalizes domain knowledge in three machine-readable layers: (1) a structured JSON schema produced by the Parser Stage capturing entities (suppliers, roasteries, cafes), constraints (capacity limits, demand requirements, e.g., close_plant) and the optimization objective (task_type minimize/maximize), serving as a validated contract between user intent and solver execution; (2) code templates constraining the Coder Stage's Z3 Python generation, including explicit constraint-handling rules (Fig. 3: plant close/open constraints mapped to solver.add(open[plant_id] == 0/1); UNSAT handling prints 'UNSAT'); and (3) the generated Z3 optimization model (Fig. 2: Optimize() solver, Int decision variables, solver.add constraints, solver.minimize(total_cost)), which encodes the domain's structure and rules and is executed by the Z3 SMT solver to compute optimal solutions.
column155: True. Defined test items, metric and procedure are all stated. Section III.D: 'The evaluation benchmark comprises 687 optimization problems across three domains... derived from the publicly available OptiGuide repository [15]' (Coffee Supply Chain 273, Facility Location 165, Workforce Scheduling 249; Table I). Section III.E: 'Performance is measured by accuracy: the proportion of questions for which the model's final parsed answer matches the ground-truth optimal value', with explicit rules that failed executions, unsatisfiable results and unparseable outputs count as incorrect. Procedure: four LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok-Code-Fast-1) accessed via the OpenRouter API are evaluated under both the LLMFP baseline and the PCV framework across all domains (Sections III.C-III.D; results in Tables II-III).
column157: benchmark: the test instrument reuses a public benchmark from prior work - the 687 problems are 'derived from the publicly available OptiGuide repository [15] (github.com/microsoft/OptiGuide)' (Section III.D). Scoring is exact-match accuracy against pre-computed ground-truth optimal values (Section III.E: 'A response is counted as correct only if the numerical answer is exactly equal to the reference solution'), a generic correctness metric, so rubric and domain-specific-metric do not apply; ground truth is reference optima rather than expert or practitioner decisions, so expert-ground-truth does not apply. ? Minor uncertainty: 'derived from' may involve author selection/adaptation of OptiGuide scenarios (the three domains 'were selected to cover diverse constraint types'), but the paper presents the set as reuse of the public OptiGuide benchmark rather than a newly authored test set.
column158: 687 optimization problems across three domains derived from the public OptiGuide repository: Coffee Supply Chain (273 questions; multi-stage capacitated network flow with 3 suppliers, 2 roasteries, 3 cafes and continuous variables), Facility Location (165; Capacitated Facility Location Problem with 5 plants, 4 warehouses and binary open/close decisions), and Workforce Scheduling (249; employee rostering with 7 workers over 14 days and time-based constraints). Four state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok-Code-Fast-1) selected via the OpenRouter API were evaluated under both the LLMFP baseline (Table II) and the PCV framework (Table III). Metric: accuracy - a response is correct only if the parsed numerical answer exactly equals the ground-truth optimal value; failed executions, unsatisfiable results and unparseable outputs count as incorrect (Section III.E).
column166: information-analysis: the LLM stages interpret the given problem and generate the formal solution model - the Parser 'performs semantic extraction' of entities, constraints and the optimization objective, and the Coder 'transforms this JSON specification into executable Z3 Python code' (Section III.B), integrating and interpreting the problem instance (intelligence/design). decision-selection: the Z3 solver driven by the system evaluates the feasible space and computes the single optimal solution to the planning problem, which the system returns as its final answer (Section III.A: 'The system then executes this code in a secure environment and returns the raw output, which the model interprets into a natural language answer'; Section III.E: answers matched against 'the ground-truth optimal value'). information-acquisition does not apply: no retrieval over documents/databases, web/API search, or sensor/ERP queries beyond the given problem instance are described; the Parser only encodes the supplied question and domain context. action-implementation does not apply: the system returns/reports the computed optimal answer but does not write the selected decision into a real-world plan, model or production system.
column168: 2-recommendation: the system, via the Z3 solver, actively evaluates alternatives and computes the single optimal solution to the planning problem, presenting it as its final answer - it selects and presents one preferred option rather than merely listing candidates for the human to rank (Section III.A: 'The system then executes this code in a secure environment and returns the raw output, which the model interprets into a natural language answer'). It does not implement the selected decision in any real-world plan or system (the answer is returned/reported, not enacted), so autonomy does not reach 3-veto or 4-autonomous. The paper frames deployment as decision support: 'LLM-based optimization is viable for decision-support deployment' (Section IV.C), leaving final adoption of the decision to the human.
column170: Partially. §III describes the architecture in reasonable detail: PCV's three stages (§III.B: 'The Parser Stage performs semantic extraction... The Coder Stage performs code synthesis... The Validator Stage... acts as a static analyzer'), the LLMFP baseline (§III.A), the four models selected via OpenRouter (§III.C), the benchmark source (§III.D: 'derived from the publicly available OptiGuide repository'), and the evaluation metric (§III.E). However, no verbatim prompts are disclosed—only stage descriptions and figure excerpts (Fig. 1: 'Sequential role-based prompting (3 API calls to same LLM)')—and no decoding parameters or implementation repository are provided, so independent replication of the exact pipeline is not fully supported. Minor internal inconsistency noted: §III.A states 'The PCV pipeline proceeds through six stages' while actually describing the LLMFP loop (PCV has three stages per §III.B), suggesting a typo.
column172: Partially (category A: implemented-validated; experiments run on 687 problems with 4 models). The metric is operationally defined (§III.E: 'Performance is measured by accuracy: the proportion of questions for which the model's final parsed answer matches the ground-truth optimal value... counted as correct only if the numerical answer is exactly equal to the reference solution'), sample sizes are reported (Table I: 273 Coffee, 165 Facility, 249 Workforce = 687), and a comparator is used (LLMFP baseline vs PCV, Tables II–III). Reported figures are internally consistent with textual claims (e.g., Grok LLMFP mean 52.72% vs PCV 92.43% = '+39.71%'; 'worst PCV configuration (87.20%)' matches GPT-OSS-20B's PCV mean). Missing: no variance, repeated runs, or statistical analysis are reported—results appear to be single-run accuracies—so the Yes bar is not met.
column174: Partially. Failure modes and scope are discussed extensively: §IV.A identifies 'Three primary failure modes... syntax errors..., parsing failures..., and semantic errors', §IV.B notes a PCV regression ('GPT-OSS-20B regresses by 3.97%'), and the conclusions reiterate the error taxonomy ('most of LLMFP failures are formatting errors, not reasoning failures'). Future work acknowledges scope limits (cross-lingual evaluation, larger models). However, threats to the validity of the evaluation itself—e.g., single-run variance, benchmark selection bias, or the extraction parser marking correct answers as failures as a measurement-validity threat—are not explicitly discussed; the parser issue ('models frequently solve problems correctly but return answers in unstructured formats, which extraction scripts mark as failures') is framed only as an LLMFP failure mode motivating PCV, not as a limitation of the study's own measurement.

column18: The paper proposes a novel agentic-AI + RAG framework for structurally adapting simulation-based digital twins and evaluates it in a controlled laboratory setting rather than in operational practice. Abstract: 'The proposed framework is evaluated in an empirical study based on data from an IoT-Factory - a laboratory assembly environment.' Section 4.1 describes controlled experiments: two adaptation scenarios 'executed five times per design choice' with defined metrics (success rate, total token usage, peak context size), plus five comparison scenarios reused from prior work, yielding 14 evaluated scenarios (Table 1). Although the underlying SBDT was auto-generated from real event logs of a physical lab factory, the framework itself was not used by real production planners in operational use - Section 5 explicitly states 'further evaluation on real-world cases with production planners is needed.' Hence validation-research (lab/artificial setting, not yet used in practice). Minor uncertainty (?): the case is built on real factory event-log data from a physical IoT-Factory, which could arguably lean toward evaluation-research, but the evaluation protocol is a controlled repeated-scenario experiment in a university laboratory, and the authors themselves classify real-world evaluation as future work.
column20: A working system is implemented (Smolagents framework with five specialized code agents, modular RAG pipeline, Qwen3-32B model, OFacT platform; Section 3) and evaluated under a defined protocol with defined quantitative metrics. Section 4.1: 'Metrics included success rate, total token usage, and peak context size' and 'We measured total modification time (end-to-end adaptation duration) and user interaction time (time spent composing prompts and reviewing responses) and success rates'; each design-choice scenario was 'executed five times per design choice'. Quantitative results are reported in Table 1 (success rates, max context size, token usage across 14 scenario executions) and Figure 2 (total/user-interaction times across five scenarios). Per decision rule 'prototype + controlled evaluation -> implemented-validated'.

column26: No research questions are explicitly stated anywhere in the paper (no RQ1/RQ2 formulation, no questions section). column28: The paper's method enables structural (re)design of a production system within a single factory: an LLM-based design assistant adapts the auto-generated digital twin of the IoT-Factory laboratory by adding/removing assembly stations, stationary resources, product features, and value-added processes (Abstract; §1; §4.1). This maps to factory planning per VDI 5200 (design/redesign of a production line within one site); the keyword list explicitly includes 'Production system design'. column52: An LLM-based design assistant enables non-simulation experts (production planners) to structurally adapt simulation-based digital-twin (SBDT) models of material-flow/production systems during (re)design through natural-language interaction. Input: a natural-language modification goal (e.g., add a humidity-sensor feature to the product structure, or add a new assembly station with associated parts and process execution plans). The agentic AI system - a hierarchical multi-agent architecture implemented with the Smolagents framework, combined with an adaptive RAG pipeline over OpenFactoryTwin (OFacT) documentation and state-model data - plans and executes the adaptations (creating, deleting, merging and modifying model elements) on the open-source OFacT digital-twin platform via a digital-twin software interface, replacing expert-authored framework-specific step instructions. Output: the modified digital-twin model plus a task summary returned to the user; the assistant serves as decision support allowing design-phase model adaptation without simulation expertise.
column54: Only Qwen3-32B is deployed and evaluated with the paper's own method: Section 4.1 states 'All tests used the Qwen3-32B model', covering both the design-variant study (agent cardinality, planning methodology, model class; Table 1) and the comparison with the prior framework (Section 4.3). Design Variant 3 contrasts foundation vs. reasoning-enhanced LLMs (Section 4.1) but names no additional models - presumably Qwen3-32B run with vs. without its reasoning mode (?). No other LLMs are named anywhere in the paper (related-work citations [5,14-16,19,20] mention no specific models), so there are no discussed-but-not-deployed models to record.
column55: Qwen3-32B is the single underlying LLM for all agents (main coordinating agent; delete/merge/modify/summarize code agents; Create Object tool agent) and all evaluation runs. Variant 3 (model class) compared reasoning-enhanced vs. foundation (no-reasoning) behavior; since Section 4.1 states all tests used Qwen3-32B, this presumably reflects toggling the model's reasoning mode rather than using different models.

column74: Section 3: 'A hierarchical design employs five specialized code agents: The main agent coordinates and delegates tasks, while the other four agents handle the operations of deleting, merging, modifying of model elements as well as summarizing the overall task', plus a dedicated Create Object tool agent. A controlling main agent delegates work to specialized sub-agents at run time, i.e., a supervisor hierarchy. Note: Variant 1 of the evaluation also tested one-agent and many-agent cardinalities (Section 4.1), but the final framework retains the hierarchical supervisor design (Section 4.2: the lean setup with specialized tools achieved the highest success rates).
column76: Orchestrator-workers: the main agent breaks adaptation tasks down and delegates them at run time to the specialized delete/merge/modify/summarize code agents and the Create Object tool agent (Section 3). Routing: the adaptive RAG pipeline includes a router module that 'dynamically decides when and how to retrieve' (Section 3), classifying queries toward specialized retrieval/generation modules; the paper does not explicitly state whether this router is an LLM call, but the agentic dynamic-decision framing suggests it (?). The pipeline also lists a judge module, but no generate-evaluate feedback loop is described, so evaluator-optimizer is not coded.
column80: Memory: the ReAct agents accumulate reasoning, actions and observations within a task/session, and the evaluation reports peak context sizes up to ~19,662 tokens within single runs (Table 1), indicating short-term working memory; no persistent cross-session memory store is described. Planning: the main agent coordinates and delegates tasks (Section 3), and the planning methodology selected for the final framework is a RAG-driven planner whose 'plans [are] synthesized directly from retrieved context' (Sections 4.1-4.2); the compared ADaPT variant additionally uses a dedicated planning agent with dynamic task decomposition - an LLM component thus explicitly plans before execution. Tool use: the Smolagents-based code agents and the dedicated Create Object tool agent decide and invoke operations/tools at run time following the ReAct pattern (Section 3).
column82: RAG: an explicit retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (router, retriever, query rewriter, generator, post-processor, judge, and a specialized Find Object module) over OFacT documentation and state-model data, preprocessed via structured indexing and embeddings (Section 3; Abstract). Digital-twin: the system adapts the OFacT simulation-based digital-twin model through the digital twin software interface and the Find Object module interacting with the state model (Section 3). Code-execution: the method is implemented with the Smolagents framework and employs 'five specialized code agents' alongside tool agents (Section 3); Smolagents code agents generate and execute Python actions (cf. Section 2.3 citing [20] on Python-based actions for flexible execution). OFacT is the digital twin being adapted, not an external simulation platform called by the LLM system, so simulation-platform is not coded; no solver, non-LLM ML model, SQL generation, enterprise system, CAD/GIS tool, or web API is called.
column84: The proposed method is an LLM-based, agentic design assistant that performs structural adaptations of digital-twin models (adding features, adding assembly stations, deleting/merging/modifying model elements) via natural-language interaction and a RAG pipeline (§3). It does not itself formulate or solve any optimization/OR problem. Optimization appears only in the introduction/abstract as the general purpose of simulation-based digital twins ('efficient and holistic optimization of material-flow systems', Abstract, §1) and in related work on parameterized models coupled with search/optimization algorithms (§2.1) — i.e., background context, not the method's own contribution. The evaluation metrics are success rate, token usage, peak context size, and modification/user-interaction times (§4.1), not optimization objectives or solver outcomes.
column86: Since the proposed method performs no optimization, the formalization level is 'none'. The assistant's tasks — e.g., adding a humidity-sensor feature to a feature cluster or adding a new assembly station with parts and process execution plans (§4.1) — are discrete modeling operations on a digital-twin state model, not formalized problems with decision variables, objective functions, or constraints.
column88: No optimization paradigm applies because the method itself performs no optimization; the paradigm set is therefore empty. The underlying OFacT platform supports 'simulation-based design of MFS' (§2.3/§3), but the proposed assistant only adapts the simulation/digital-twin model structure and never executes a simulation-optimization loop, metaheuristic, RL search, MCDM ranking, or solver call.
column91: There is no optimizer in the method for the LLM to interact with, so the role is 'none'. The LLM (Qwen3-32B, §4.1) operates as an agentic modeling assistant: a hierarchical multi-agent system (Smolagents framework, §3) retrieves documentation/state-model context via RAG and executes model modifications (delete, merge, modify, create-object tool agents). It neither formulates optimization models, proposes/improves solutions to an optimization problem, designs optimization heuristics, orchestrates a solver, interprets optimization results, nor verifies optimization solutions.
column93: No optimization solver is mentioned or used anywhere in the paper; the method involves no solver invocation of any kind (no Gurobi, CPLEX, CP solver, etc.). Solver type is therefore NR (not reported).
column96: All evaluation episodes are performed on a single case: the auto-generated SBDT of the IoT-Factory laboratory assembly environment at HSBI (§4.1), so 'single-case' applies. No user study with external participants, no test set/benchmark, and no field deployment are reported.

Although the SBDT is auto-generated from real factory event logs, the episodes are lab sessions on constructed tasks rather than a real organisation's pending redesign problem addressed with real users; the authors confirm this by stating that 'further evaluation on real-world cases with production planners is needed' (§5).

column140: The proposed agentic-AI framework with a RAG pipeline performs structural adaptations of digital-twin models without expert-authored, framework-specific step instructions, achieving high adaptation success rates with substantially fewer DT-specific requirements. In the design-choice evaluation on the IoT-Factory SBDT (§4.1 notes all tests used the Qwen3-32B model): a lean multi-agent setup with specialized tools achieved the highest success rates (0.8 on both scenarios), while replacing those tools with additional agents reduced success due to coordination overhead; the RAG-driven planner matched ADaPT on the simple feature scenario (both 0.8) and outperformed it on the complex assembly-station scenario (1.0 vs. 0.4) with more efficient context usage, and was therefore selected for the final framework; foundation (no-reasoning) LLMs outperformed reasoning-enhanced LLMs on both scenarios (1.0 vs. 0.6 and 0.8 vs. 0.2), with deliberative models deviating more often from plans and consuming more tokens. Compared with the previous step-instruction-based framework across five reused scenarios, user-interaction and total modification times showed negligible differences (except that the new framework required more user time in the most complex Scenario 5, likely due to an additional validation step); both frameworks achieved 100% success on the simpler adding-feature scenario, while the former framework was slightly more reliable on the more complex adding-value-added-process scenario (80% vs. 60%), plausibly because detailed step instructions constrained the agent's behavior, reducing flexibility but also modelling errors.
column143: True. The assistant works through multi-turn natural-language dialogue in which the user reviews system output inside the workflow and steers subsequent steps. §1: it 'performs modeling through natural-language interaction with non-expert users'; §4.1 defines user interaction time as 'time spent composing prompts and reviewing responses' (plural prompts/responses, indicating an iterative review-and-steer loop rather than a single query plus final read). §4.3 additionally reports for the complex scenario 'an additional validation step to ensure alignment with the user's intent', i.e., the user actively checks the system's output against their intent. ? It is not specified whether review/validation gates the modification before it is applied or occurs afterwards, and the validation step is introduced only as a likely explanation ('likely due to') for higher user times.

The 'validation step to ensure alignment with the user's intent' (§4.3) could additionally amount to an approval-gate, but it is mentioned only speculatively ('likely due to') and without procedural detail, so it is noted here rather than coded (?).

column151: mathematical-model: the simulation-based digital twin of the production system — a 'dynamic behavior space capturing real or simulated process executions' over the state model (§2.3) — is a simulation model of the planning domain whose structure the agentic system adapts ('structural adaptation of digital-twin models', Abstract). structured-schema: the OFacT 'static configuration space (state model) defining entities, resources, and processes' (§2.3) is a non-graph schema of domain entities that the system queries (Find Object module, §3) and indexes for retrieval ('state-model data are preprocessed via structured indexing', §3). column152: Domain knowledge is formalized in the OFacT digital twin: (i) a static configuration space (state model) defining the entities, resources and processes of the production system, which the agentic system queries via a specialized Find Object module and which is preprocessed via structured indexing and embeddings for RAG; and (ii) a dynamic behavior space capturing real or simulated process executions, making the digital twin a simulation model of the material-flow system (§2.3, §3). (2) Framework comparison — five scenarios of increasing complexity reused from prior work (adding a new feature; adding a stationary resource; modifying a transition model; creating a value-added process; a composite operation combining all prior modifications), measuring total modification time, user interaction time and success rates (scenarios 1 and 2 executed five times each for success rates); all tests used the Qwen3-32B model (§4.1, §4.3).

column166: information-acquisition: at run time the system retrieves context beyond the user's request — the RAG pipeline 'dynamically decides when and how to retrieve' with 'a router, retriever (vector- or graph-based), query rewriter, generator, post-processor, judge, and a specialized Find Object module for interacting with the digital twin's state model', over 'Documentation and state-model data... preprocessed via structured indexing and embeddings' (§3); it 'relies exclusively on publicly available information from the open-source digital-twin platform OpenFactoryTwin (OFacT)' (Abstract). information-analysis: the agentic system interprets the modification goal and generates the adaptation plan — 'a dedicated planning agent with dynamic task decomposition' vs. 'plans synthesized directly from retrieved context' (§4.1), with reasoning following 'the ReAct pattern (reasoning, action, observation)' (§3). action-implementation: the agents themselves write the redesign into the digital-twin model — 'the other four agents handle the operations of deleting, merging, modifying of model elements... Objects are created separately through a dedicated Create Object tool agent' (§3); the assistant 'performs modeling' and executes adaptations (Abstract, §1). decision-selection is not automated: the production expert specifies the modification goal (Fig. 1: 'Production Expert' → 'Modification Goal'), and the system does not evaluate or rank alternative redesign options.
column168: 3-veto. Once the user states a modification goal, the agentic system autonomously works out and implements the structural adaptation in the digital twin — the agents directly 'handle the operations of deleting, merging, modifying of model elements' and create objects (§3); the assistant 'performs modeling' (Abstract) — i.e., it decides and implements without a prior human approval step. The human nevertheless retains veto/correction power inside the workflow: interaction is a multi-turn natural-language dialogue in which the user reviews responses and composes follow-up prompts (§4.1: 'time spent composing prompts and reviewing responses'), and the new framework adds 'a validation step to ensure alignment with the user's intent' (§4.3). Hence the system decides and implements unless the human vetoes/corrects, rather than being fully autonomous. ? The paper does not state whether validation precedes or follows implementation; if user review were purely post-hoc reading of final results, 4-autonomous could be argued.

column11: Proceedings of the 40th ACM SIGSIM International Conference on Principles of Advanced Discrete Simulation
column18: The paper proposes three design principles and the FactoryFlow framework, then empirically evaluates them in a controlled, artificial setting: a benchmark set of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35) is processed through the LLM pipeline, generated models are compared against researcher-constructed ground-truth implementations at the component/connection/parameter levels, and errors are classified per an eight-type taxonomy (Sections 5.1-5.3, Figures 2-4). Because the evaluation uses constructed benchmark models rather than operational industrial use or real company data, this is validation-research rather than evaluation-research. It is not a bare solution-proposal because a thorough empirical evaluation is present (e.g., the netlist-vs-Python-IR error comparison in Section 5.3), and not a philosophical paper because the taxonomy and design principles are grounded in and supported by quantitative experiments. Evidence: Section 5.1, 'We constructed a benchmark set of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35) with varying sizes and topological complexity.'
column20: FactoryFlow is a working, publicly released open-source implementation (GitHub repository cited; DataFITR and FactoryFlow GUI screenshots in Appendix B; LangGraph-based pipeline using Gemini 2.5 Pro described in Section 3), and it is evaluated under a defined protocol with defined metrics: 35 benchmark models with ground-truth implementations, coarse and detailed description variants, error counts per the eight-category taxonomy, and structural/semantic model comparison (Section 5.1). Quantitative results are reported (Figures 2-4; e.g., S8 netlist IR: 10 errors vs Python IR: 2 errors). This satisfies 'working system + evaluation under a defined protocol with defined metrics' -> implemented-validated. Anchor (Section 5.1): 'The generated FactorySimPy models were compared against ground-truth implementations at the component, connection, and parameter levels.'
column22: The paper explicitly scopes to manufacturing: 'discrete-event simulation (DES) models of manufacturing systems' (Section 1, Problem Definition and Scope), citing 'assembly lines, packaging lines, semiconductor fabrication facilities, and consumer goods production plants.' The Abstract describes FactoryFlow as 'an open-source, LLM-assisted framework for building simulation-based Digital Twins of manufacturing systems.'
column23: Manufacturing systems (discrete-event simulation models for Digital Twins)
column24: The evaluation domain is DES models of manufacturing systems: the 35 benchmark models include simple serial systems, parallel systems with feedback loops, multi-edge systems with routing policies, hierarchical/nested subsystems, irregular interconnections, and very large regular structures such as 100-machine lines and grids (Section 5.1). Note: this is a constructed benchmark study, not an industrial case study on real company data; the authors additionally report generating hierarchical manufacturing lines with >10,000 components beyond the benchmark set (Section 4, Principle 3).
column25: Section 5.3 states four key questions guiding the error analysis: (1) How do error counts correlate with model size and complexity? (2) Which error types are most frequent, and does this vary between coarse and detailed descriptions? (3) What is the impact of description granularity on error profiles? (4) Are certain model characteristics or description styles more error-prone?
column26: The paper does not pose formal numbered RQs in the introduction, but Section 5.3 explicitly enumerates the questions structuring the empirical analysis: 'We analyze the LLM-generated models to address four key questions: (1) How do error counts correlate with model size and complexity? (2) Which error types are most frequent, and does this vary between coarse and detailed descriptions? (3) What is the impact of description granularity on error profiles? (4) Are certain model characteristics or description styles more error-prone?' These are analysis questions for the error-characterization study rather than overarching paper RQs; the broader motivating challenge (resilience to LLM hallucination plus systematic human oversight in LLM-assisted Digital Twin modeling) is stated in the Abstract and Section 1.
column28: Mapped by task description (Appendix A): the paper's method (FactoryFlow) generates executable discrete-event simulation (DES) models of manufacturing production systems — 'assembly lines, packaging lines, semiconductor fabrication facilities, and consumer goods production plants' (§1) — composed of machines, buffers, conveyors, sources/sinks (§3–4). Simulation modeling of production systems falls under factory-planning. Boundary case (?): the paper frames its digital twins primarily for operational use ('adapt continuously to real-time sensor data', 'ongoing monitoring and adaptation... and control', §1), with structural changes handled sporadically ('equipment upgrades, line reconfigurations, capacity expansions', §1); the factory-planning dimension enters via what-if analysis support for such structural changes, which is stated generically (§1) but not demonstrated as a planning application. No other subdomain (SC-network, logistics/distribution, technology selection, site selection, GPN) is addressed.
column31: Core task is simulation modeling: 'FactoryFlow is an open-source framework for generating executable discrete-event simulation models of manufacturing Digital Twins from coarse natural language descriptions and sensor data' (§3). The LLM-based flow translates natural-language structure descriptions into DES models (§3), DataFITR performs continuous distribution fitting/parameter inference from sensor streams (§3–4), and §5 characterizes errors in the generated simulation models. The method itself performs no other planning task: capacity expansions/line reconfigurations appear only as structural changes the models must represent (§1), not as tasks the method executes.
column33: The models and decision support concern production: 'discrete-event simulation (DES) models of manufacturing systems' with parameters such as 'machine task delays, energy profiles, state transition rates, failure rates' (§1); modeled components are machines, buffers, conveyors, splitters/mergers, sources/sinks (§3–4). This is the production process (plants, lines, capacities) of the SCP Matrix. Procurement, distribution, and sales processes are neither modeled nor addressed.
column35: The paper never references VDI 5200; the phase mapping is inferred from the simulation-modeling task (?). The generated DES models represent production-system structure, interconnections, and capacities, and the DTs provide 'what-if analysis' decision support (§1) for planned structural changes — 'equipment upgrades, line reconfigurations, capacity expansions' (§1) — corresponding to concept planning (structure, dimensioning, variants; primary mapping) and detailed planning (models carry detailed component parameters and interconnections; secondary mapping) of such changes. Strong uncertainty (?): the paper's primary framing is operational digital twins (real-time adaptation, control); support for concept/detailed planning phases is implicit via the generic what-if statement and is not demonstrated within a factory planning process. Flag for verifier attention.
column37: No planning horizon (e.g., '5 years') is stated anywhere in the paper. Only relative temporal qualifiers are used, describing sensor streams and change frequency ('real-time', 'continuous', 'sporadic', 'infrequent' — §1, §4), not a planning horizon.
column40: Operational: the DTs 'adapt continuously to real-time sensor data' with 'continuous fitting and tuning to sensor data, ongoing monitoring and adaptation, and model-based decision support including what-if analysis, optimization, and control' (§1) — short-term monitoring/control decisions are the primary demonstrated use. Strategic: selected because system_configuring_decision is judged true; the stated decision support ('what-if analysis, optimization', §1) applied to the workflow's structural scope — 'changes to equipment interconnections, active machines, job sequencing and routing' and 'structural changes are infrequent and typically planned (equipment upgrades, line reconfigurations, capacity expansions)' (§1) — concerns what exists in the production system. Uncertainty (?): the strategic dimension is inferred from the generic what-if/optimization statement plus the structural-change scope; the paper demonstrates model generation and error characterization, not an actual strategic decision. Tactical: not addressed; no mid-term allocation of existing resources is discussed.
column42: No claim found. The paper does not apply 'strategic', 'tactical', or 'operational' as planning-horizon labels to its decisions. 'Real-time'/'continuous' describe data streams and adaptation (§1); 'operational' appears only as a modifier of 'data'/'conditions' ('real-time operational data', 'operational conditions', §1), not as a claimed planning tier. Per D035/D060/D140, no tier is inferred from the task.
column44: True. The digital twins built by the method provide 'model-based decision support including what-if analysis, optimization, and control' (§1), and the workflow's structural scope consists of configuration-determining changes: 'changes to equipment interconnections, active machines, job sequencing and routing' and 'structural changes are infrequent and typically planned (equipment upgrades, line reconfigurations, capacity expansions)' (§1). What-if analysis/optimization over these structural dimensions determines what exists in the production system (which machines/equipment, their interconnections, capacities), as opposed to only how existing resources are used. Uncertainty (?): the configuring-decision support is inferred from the stated what-if/optimization decision support plus the structural-change scope; the paper demonstrates model generation, validation, and error characterization rather than an actual configuring decision, and the structural model can alternatively be read as tracking changes after they occur ('When structural changes occur, expert input is solicited to modify the description and regenerate the model', §4).

The authors frame the digital twins as providing 'model-based decision support including what-if analysis, optimization, and control' (§1) and as adapting to structural changes, never as designing/configuring the system. Per pilot 0.10.1, what-if analysis framing does not count as a configuring statement; no verbatim quote states that the supported decision designs, configures, selects or locates system elements.
column47: Per the paper's structural scope (§1), the what-if/optimization decision support would determine: equipment upgrades, line reconfigurations, capacity expansions, and changes to equipment interconnections, active machines, job sequencing and routing — i.e., which machines/buffers/conveyors exist in the production system, how they are interconnected, and at what capacities.
column49: No planning-domain framework structures the paper's scope. The contribution is organized around three self-derived design principles for LLM-assisted modeling workflows (§4: orthogonalizing structural modeling and parameter fitting; component-based composition; density-preserving intermediate representations) and the manufacturing digital twin concept. VDI 5200, the SC Planning Matrix, Lanza et al. 2019, Wiendahl-Nyhuis, and Melo et al. 2009 are neither cited nor used; background citations (AMG, process mining, LLMs for simulation modeling, §2) are related work, not planning frameworks structuring the scope.
column50: Required because 'none' was selected: the paper is a methodology study of LLM-assisted simulation model generation (design principles, architecture, error characterization). Its scope is structured by the authors' own design principles (§4) and the digital twin concept for manufacturing systems; no factory or supply-chain planning reference model (VDI 5200, SCP Matrix, or similar) appears in the text.
column52: FactoryFlow is an open-source, LLM-assisted framework for generating executable discrete-event simulation (DES) models of manufacturing-system Digital Twins from coarse natural-language descriptions and sensor data. The LLM's role is structural model generation: a LangGraph pipeline with two LLM nodes translates a coarse natural-language system description into (1) explicit assumptions (component identifiers, buffer counts, routing policies) via a reasoning node, and (2) executable Python code – a density-preserving intermediate representation – that instantiates and interconnects pre-validated components from the FactorySimPy library, via a code-generation node. Outputs are the Python IR model, an automatically derived block diagram for human visual validation, and an executable simulation model, with iterative human-in-the-loop refinement (users can edit the description, assumptions, or generated code and resubmit) and automated rule-based validation (detection of isolated components, missing connections, unspecified parameters, interconnection-rule violations). Parameter fitting is deliberately orthogonalized from the LLM: the non-LLM DataFITR subsystem continuously fits distributions to streaming sensor data under expert-tunable GUI controls. The LLM thereby democratizes simulation modeling for factory operators and production engineers without M&S expertise and supports Digital-Twin decision making (what-if analysis, optimization) via continuously adaptable models.
column54: Gemini 2.5 Pro is the only LLM deployed and evaluated with the paper's method: 'We use Gemini 2.5 Pro with few-shot prompting' (Section 3) and 'all experiments used a single LLM backend (Gemini 2.5 Pro)' (Section 6, Limitations). No other specific LLMs are deployed, compared, or used as baselines; multi-model comparison and smaller/locally hosted models are explicitly listed as future work (Section 6).
column55: Gemini 2.5 Pro is the single LLM backend serving both LangGraph nodes (reasoning/assumption inference and Python code generation) in the structural modeling pipeline; the DataFITR parameter-fitting subsystem explicitly does not use an LLM ('LLMs are not required; classical statistical methods and ML algorithms suffice', Section 4).
column57: Gemini 2.5 Pro belongs to Google's proprietary Gemini family, explicitly named in Section 3 and Section 6 (Limitations).
column60: Gemini 2.5 Pro is a proprietary Google model whose weights are not openly available. The paper's discussion of 'computational cost and API stability of commercial models' (Section 1) and its listing of 'locally hosted models' only as future work (Section 6) are consistent with proprietary API use.
column63: Deployment mode is not explicitly stated, but Gemini 2.5 Pro is a proprietary Google model accessible only via a hosted API; the paper frames 'computational cost and API stability of commercial models' as practical constraints of its approach (Section 1) and mentions 'cost-performance tradeoffs with smaller or locally hosted models' solely as future work (Section 6), implying API-based access (? inferred from model identity and context).
column65: The LLM receives only textual inputs: coarse/detailed natural-language system descriptions, a system prompt, the FactorySimPy API specification, and example models (Sections 3 and 5.1). Block diagrams are generated as outputs for human inspection, not consumed by the LLM; no image or other modality input is described.
column67: No weight updates are reported; the method relies solely on few-shot prompting with a system prompt and in-context examples (Section 3).
column71: 'We use Gemini 2.5 Pro with few-shot prompting that demonstrates component instantiation, interconnection patterns, parameter passing, and naming conventions' (Section 3); the code-generation node additionally receives a system prompt, the FactorySimPy API specification, and example models. No CoT, self-consistency, ReAct, or schema/grammar-constrained decoding is described for the method (grammar-constrained generation appears only in related work, Section 2).
column74: The structural modeling component uses a LangGraph architecture with two primary LLM nodes in a developer-fixed sequence: a reasoning node (interprets the description, identifies missing information, proposes explicit assumptions) followed by a code-generation node (generates the Python IR), after which deterministic validation routines and human-in-the-loop refinement run (Section 3, Figure 1). The LLM nodes do not decide their next action or tool calls at run time; the flow is fixed by the developers, matching the 'pipeline' definition (fixed, developer-defined sequence of specialised LLM roles).
column76: Prompt-chaining: the reasoning node's output (explicit assumptions) is passed to the code-generation node, which also receives the description and supporting materials – a fixed sequence of two LLM calls with distinct roles (reasoning node -> code-generation node; Section 3, Figure 1). The validation loop uses deterministic FactorySimPy rule checks plus human inspection/resubmission rather than a second LLM evaluator, so evaluator-optimizer does not apply (per 0.10.4, deterministic validation feedback is not evaluator-optimizer). No routing, parallelization, or orchestrator-workers patterns are present.
column80: Agent memory: FactoryFlow 'maintains structured state containing the user description and inferred assumptions, updated incrementally across LangGraph iterations' (Section 3) – working memory within one modeling task/session (short-term); no persistent cross-session memory is described. Planning/reflection: the reasoning node performs pre-generation assumption inference, but no LLM component plans task decomposition, self-critiques, or reflects on its own or the generator's output; error detection relies on deterministic validation routines and human visual inspection (Sections 3–5). Tool use: the LLM nodes do not decide to call tools/functions at run time; pipeline steps and execution of the generated code are developer-fixed (Section 3).
column82: Code-execution: the LLM-generated Python IR is executed – automated validation routines run on the generated model and accepted models proceed to simulation execution (Section 3; Figure 10 shows TOP.run_simulation(25)). Digital-twin: the framework is explicitly a Digital Twin modeling workflow in which the LLM-generated executable simulation model serves as the DT of the manufacturing system, with the non-LLM DataFITR subsystem continuously fitting parameters from sensor streams (Sections 1, 3, 4). No RAG (the FactorySimPy API specification and examples are supplied in-prompt as few-shot context, not retrieved from a store), no solver, no ML-model called by the LLM (DataFITR is an orthogonal non-LLM subsystem not invoked by the LLM pipeline), no database-SQL, enterprise-system, CAD-GIS, or web-search integrations. FactorySimPy is the library the generated model is written against – the model is itself the simulation – so it is not coded as an external simulation platform (D111).
column84: The proposed method (FactoryFlow) generates executable discrete-event simulation (DES) models of manufacturing systems from natural language descriptions via an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro, LangGraph pipeline, §3) and performs statistical distribution fitting on sensor streams (DataFITR, §3–4); it neither formulates nor solves an optimization/OR problem. Optimization appears only as motivating context in the introduction (§1: 'model-based decision support including what-if analysis, optimization, and control') and as planned future work (§6: 'Automated design space exploration and optimization capabilities are planned as extensions in FactoryFlow'). The LLM-generated models are simulation models that are executed and validated, not optimization models that are solved, and the generate-refine loop produces model code rather than iteratively improving optimization solutions.
column86: No optimization tradition is present, so the formalization level is 'none'. The paper's contributions are three design principles for LLM-assisted simulation model generation (§4), an eight-category error taxonomy with empirical characterization over 35 benchmark models (§5), and expert-tunable statistical parameter fitting (DataFITR, §4 Principle 1). No objective function, decision variables, or constraints of an optimization problem are stated by the method itself.
column88: Empty set: the method performs no optimization, so no paradigm applies. DataFITR's distribution fitting is classical statistical estimation on sensor data ('classical statistical methods and ML algorithms suited to time-series analysis', §4 Principle 1), not simulation-optimization; the DES models are run for validation and what-if purposes only, and design-space exploration/optimization is explicitly deferred to future work (§6).
column91: There is no optimizer in the method, so the LLM's role relative to an optimizer is 'none' (per D075/D079). The LLM translates natural language system descriptions into Python code instantiating FactorySimPy simulation components (§3) — simulation model generation, not formulation of an optimization model or solver code. No solver call, solution interpretation, or LLM-based optimization verification is involved; structural validation is performed by automated rule-based routines in FactorySimPy, not by the LLM.
column93: No optimization solver is used or mentioned anywhere in the paper. The framework relies on SimPy-based discrete-event simulation (FactorySimPy) and statistical distribution fitting (DataFITR); no MILP/NLP/CP or other OR solver is invoked, so the solver type is NR.
column96: The paper's own evaluation is an error-characterization study on an author-built benchmark of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35), each processed with both coarse and detailed natural-language descriptions through the FactoryFlow LLM pipeline and scored against ground-truth implementations (Section 5.1). The netlist-vs-Python IR comparison (Section 5.3) is an ablation of the method's own IR component within this test set, not a separate study design; no user study, case deployment, or field evaluation is reported.
column98: All evaluation episodes use author-constructed benchmark models, author-written ground-truth Python implementations, and author-prepared natural-language descriptions (Section 5.1: 'We constructed a benchmark set of 35 manufacturing system models... we prepared three artifacts'). No real users, real organisations, or real operational data are involved, so the evaluation is artificial per FEDS.
column99: Author-built benchmark of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35) with ground-truth Python implementations, coarse and detailed natural-language descriptions, LLM-generated outputs, identified errors, and analysis scripts; publicly available in the FactoryFlow GitHub repository.
column100: Section 5.1: 'We constructed a benchmark set of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35) with varying sizes and topological complexity'; Section 5 states the dataset 'is publicly available in the FactoryFlow GitHub repository'. This is not a reused public benchmark but an author-built test set.
column102: The only comparisons in the evaluation are (a) generated models vs. author-written ground-truth implementations and (b) netlist-based IR vs. Python-based IR, which is an ablation of the method's own IR component (Section 5.3). Per schema definitions, neither counts as a comparator; no alternative method, human-planner baseline, conventional tool, or prior AI/ML system was applied to the same tasks.
column106: No Python syntax errors observed across all 35 benchmark models; errors were confined to naming, parameters, hallucinations, and FactorySimPy framework constraints detectable by automated validation.
column111: S5, a simple linear sequence of 5 machines (7 nodes, 6 edges, 12 parameters); the netlist representation (13 dictionary entries) generated zero errors with detailed descriptions, indicating enumerative IR remains adequate at small scale.
column116: S8, a linear system with additional buffers inserted at specific positions; netlist-based IR produced 10 errors including structural hallucinations, incorrect parameter assignments, FactorySimPy constraint violations, and improper edge chaining.
column121: The same model S8 generated with Python-based IR produced only 2 errors, versus 10 with netlist-based IR.
column126: S35 (112 nodes, 165 edges with parallel and serial structures, 278 netlist entries); netlist-based IR hallucinated 10 nodes not in the description due to explicit enumeration of repeated subsystems.

Figures 2-4 present per-model error counts and aggregate error-type frequencies graphically, but exact numeric values beyond those listed are not stated in the text. No aggregate accuracy/precision percentages, timings, or cost figures are reported.
