column139: Section 6 ('Limitations') explicitly lists these limitations, covering approach-inherent constraints (static-structure assumption, component-library rigidity), characterization-study scope (single LLM backend, no multi-run averaging, manufacturing-only scope), and ongoing implementation work (structural change detection, real-time DataFITR streaming).
column140: Across the 35-model benchmark, error counts generally increase with model size and IR complexity, but structural regularity mitigates error accumulation even at scale (S31-S35, with 100+ components, show comparatively lower error rates due to regular repeated structures). No Python syntax errors (T7) occurred across all 35 models, confirming that component-based composition confines errors to naming, parameters, hallucinations, and framework constraints detectable by automated validation. Coarse descriptions produce errors dominated by naming (T1) and hallucinations (T3-T5), while detailed descriptions reduce naming errors but increase hierarchy mismatches (T6) and FactorySimPy violations (T8). The netlist-vs-Python IR comparison validates the density-preservation principle: for S8, netlist IR produced 10 errors versus 2 with Python IR; for S35 (112 nodes, 165 edges), netlist IR hallucinated 10 nodes and 7 edges, while compact loop-based Python IR substantially reduced hallucination errors and remained human-readable at scales where netlists become impractical to review.
column143: True. Human oversight of LLM output is a core design goal, and the workflow requires the human to act on the LLM's intermediate output (inspect, correct, accept) before it proceeds. §3 'Generated Model and Validation Support': the generated model 'is returned to the user along with an automatically derived block diagram for visual inspection. The user has multiple options for refinement: directly modify the generated Python code, edit the original natural language description, adjust the inferred assumptions, or any combination thereof. Modified inputs can be resubmitted to the LangGraph pipeline, enabling iterative refinement until the model satisfies domain requirements. Once the user accepts the generated model, automated validation routines execute...'. Abstract: structural descriptions are 'LLM-translated from coarse natural language to an intermediate representation (IR) with human visualization and validation'.
column145: approval-gate (workflow-initiated): human acceptance is required before the pipeline proceeds to validation/execution — 'Once the user accepts the generated model, automated validation routines execute' (§3). escalation-protocol (system-initiated): the reasoning node 'interprets the system description, identifies missing information, and proposes explicit assumptions (component identifiers, buffer counts, routing policies)' (§3); these detected gaps are surfaced to the user as editable fields in the GUI (Fig. 9: 'Editable assumptions' panel with 'Regenerate model with changes') for review/adjustment. iterative-feedback: the human judges each iteration's output and steers the next — 'Modified inputs can be resubmitted to the LangGraph pipeline, enabling iterative refinement until the model satisfies domain requirements' (§3). human-override: the human directly edits the agents' intermediate outputs — 'directly modify the generated Python code... adjust the inferred assumptions' (§3).
column146: The LLM-based structural modeling pipeline (LangGraph with a reasoning node and a code-generation node) returns the generated Python model together with an automatically derived block diagram for visual inspection. The reasoning node identifies missing information in the user's description and proposes explicit assumptions (component identifiers, buffer counts, routing policies), which are presented as editable fields in the GUI. The user can refine by directly modifying the generated Python code, editing the original natural-language description, adjusting the inferred assumptions, or any combination, and resubmit for iterative regeneration until the model satisfies domain requirements. Only after user acceptance do automated validation routines run (detecting isolated components, missing connections, unspecified mandatory parameters, and violations of FactorySimPy interconnection rules). Target users are factory operators, production engineers, and simulation experts: non-M&S users interact via the natural-language description and block diagram, while simulation experts may additionally inspect or edit the Python IR directly. On the parameter side (DataFITR), experts configure data filters, time windows, candidate distribution families, and sensor-to-parameter mappings through GUI-based controls, under which automated fitting runs continuously with manual configuration available when needed.
column149: True. Manufacturing domain knowledge is encoded in FactorySimPy, an explicit, reusable, machine-readable Python component library that the system uses to constrain generation, validate output, and execute models. §3: 'FactorySimPy as a validated library of configurable manufacturing system components'; the code-generation node receives 'supporting materials (FactorySimPy API specification, example models, system prompt)'; automated validation detects 'violations of component interconnection rules defined in the FactorySimPy library'. §4 Principle 2: 'FactorySimPy provides pre-validated, well-documented component classes for elements commonly found in manufacturing systems: machines with various processing policies, buffers with configurable capacities and queueing disciplines, conveyors, material handling fleets, splitters, mergers, and sources/sinks.' This is more than free-text prompts or few-shot examples: the library's component semantics and interconnection rules mechanically constrain and validate LLM output.
column151: code-template: FactorySimPy is a code library of pre-validated, parameterized component classes encoding manufacturing domain structure — a simulation blueprint. The LLM receives the FactorySimPy API specification and example models as existing domain code to adapt, and generates Python that instantiates and interconnects these components (§3; §4 Principle 2: 'restrict the model IR to interconnections of parameterized, pre-validated library components rather than monolithic simulation code'); automated validation checks generated models against interconnection rules defined in the library. No ontology, knowledge graph, standards encoding, relational database, or non-graph schema (JSON/XML/UML) is reported — the intermediate representation is Python code, not a data schema, and no optimization model with variables/constraints is used by the system.
column152: FactorySimPy is an open-source, lightweight Python library for discrete-event simulation of manufacturing systems, built on SimPy 4. It provides a well-defined set of canonical, pre-validated component classes with pre-built, configurable behavior — machines with configurable processing delays and policies, buffers with configurable capacities and queueing disciplines, conveyors, material handling fleets, splitters, mergers, and sources/sinks — together with defined component interconnection rules (e.g., one-to-one edge cardinality, port-type compatibility). The LLM-based structural generator is constrained to instantiating and interconnecting these library components (Principle 2), receives the FactorySimPy API specification and example models as supporting materials for few-shot prompting, and automated validation routines check generated models against the library's rules (isolated components, missing connections, duplicate instance names, invalid edge cardinality, incompatible connections, unsupported routing specifications). The library is extensible by subclassing existing components (an M&S-expert workflow).
column155: True. §5.1 (Methodology) describes an explicit, repeatable protocol with defined test items, defined metrics, and a stated procedure: 'We constructed a benchmark set of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35) with varying sizes and topological complexity'; for each system three artifacts were prepared (a ground-truth FactorySimPy implementation, a coarse description, a detailed description); 'Each description (coarse and detailed) was processed through FactoryFlow's LLM-based pipeline, generating assumptions and intermediate representation (IR) code. The generated FactorySimPy models were compared against ground-truth implementations at the component, connection, and parameter levels. Errors were identified and classified according to the taxonomy' (eight types T1-T8, Table 1). The dataset (benchmark models, descriptions, LLM outputs, identified errors, analysis scripts) is publicly available in the FactoryFlow GitHub repository.
column157: custom-test-set: the 35-model benchmark (S1-S35) with coarse/detailed descriptions and ground-truth implementations was built by the authors for this paper ('We constructed a benchmark set of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35)'), not a standardized benchmark reused from prior work. domain-specific-metric: scoring uses an eight-category, DES-modeling-specific error taxonomy (T1 naming, T2 parameter, T3 node hallucination, T4 edge hallucination, T5 parameter hallucination, T6 hierarchy mismatch, T7 Python syntax, T8 FactorySimPy violations; Table 1) with per-type and total error counts derived from component/connection/parameter-level comparison against ground truth — task/domain-specific measures, not generic accuracy/F1 and not a graded rubric.
column158: The authors constructed a benchmark of 35 manufacturing system models (S1-S35) spanning simple serial systems, parallel systems and feedback loops, multi-edge systems with routing policies, hierarchical/nested subsystems, irregular interconnections, and very large regular structures (100+ components). For each system they prepared: (1) a ground-truth Python implementation using FactorySimPy (intended structure with correct component names, connectivity, and parameter values); (2) a coarse natural-language description (high-level overview, minimal or no identifiers/parameters); (3) a detailed natural-language description (fully specifying structure, identifiers, parameters, connectivity, naming patterns). Each description variant was processed through FactoryFlow's LLM pipeline (Gemini 2.5 Pro), and generated models were compared against ground truth at the component, connection, and parameter levels, with functionally equivalent implementations treated as correct. Errors were classified into the eight-type taxonomy (T1-T8) and analyzed for correlation with model size/IR size, description granularity (coarse vs. detailed), and structural regularity; a subset of models was additionally used to compare netlist-based vs. Python-based IR error rates (e.g., S5, S8, S34, S35). The complete dataset (benchmark set, descriptions, LLM outputs, identified errors, analysis scripts) is publicly available on GitHub.
column166: information-acquisition: the DataFITR component 'operates continuously on real-time sensor streams' for parameter inference (§4 Principle 1) — run-time sensor queries/filtering with expert-configurable data filters and time windows; note the current open-source release runs on historical data with real-time streaming integration in progress (§6 Limitations). information-analysis: the LLM-based structural generator interprets the coarse description, identifies missing information, proposes assumptions, and generates the model — 'The reasoning node interprets the system description, identifies missing information, and proposes explicit assumptions' and the code-generation node generates 'executable Python code by instantiating FactorySimPy components and their interconnections' (§3); DataFITR likewise interprets sensor data via distribution fitting. action-implementation: the system itself writes the decision into an executable simulation model — the LLM generates the Python model code (§3), and DataFITR performs 'continuous fitting, updating model parameters automatically' (§4). decision-selection is not automated: the system generates candidate models but does not evaluate or rank alternatives; the human reviews, refines, and accepts ('Once the user accepts the generated model, automated validation routines execute', §3).
column168: The system generates candidate simulation models (with inferred assumptions and an auto-derived block diagram) that the human evaluates, adjusts, and must accept before validation and execution: 'The user has multiple options for refinement: directly modify the generated Python code, edit the original natural language description, adjust the inferred assumptions, or any combination thereof... Once the user accepts the generated model, automated validation routines execute' (§3). Per the schema note, generating candidates for humans to evaluate and adjust is '1-options'; the system does not select or rank among alternatives. Caveat: on the parameter side, DataFITR performs 'continuous fitting, updating model parameters automatically' under expert-configured GUI constraints (§4) — a higher-autonomy background process — but this executes a human-configured statistical estimation policy for model parameters, while the planning decision the method addresses (the Digital Twin model design, especially structure) remains human-gated.
column170: Architecture is described in replicable detail (Section 3, Figure 1): a LangGraph pipeline with a reasoning node and a code-generation node, structured state, and a named LLM ('We use Gemini 2.5 Pro with few-shot prompting'). Knowledge/data sources are identified (FactorySimPy API specification, example models, system prompt) and the component library is open-source with documentation (Figure 8). However, prompts are not given verbatim - only their assembly is described ('The code-generation node receives the description, assumptions, and supporting materials (FactorySimPy API specification, example models, system prompt)', Section 3) - and the repository inventory ('benchmark model set, natural language descriptions, LLM-generated outputs, identified errors, and analysis scripts', Section 5.1) does not explicitly include prompts. Decoding parameters are also unreported. At least one required element (verbatim prompts) is missing, so the criterion is only partly met.
column172: Study type A (implemented and validated system with empirical evaluation). Metrics are operationally defined: an 8-type error taxonomy with definitions and representative examples (Table 1) plus a comparison procedure ('The generated FactorySimPy models were compared against ground-truth implementations at the component, connection, and parameter levels... at the structural and semantic level rather than through exact code matching', Section 5.1). Sample size is reported (35 models S1-S35, each processed with coarse and detailed descriptions). Comparators/conditions are reported (ground-truth implementations; coarse vs detailed descriptions; netlist vs Python IR on S5, S8, S34, S35). Reported results (Figures 2-4, Section 5.3) support the text claims. However, no repeated runs or variance measures are reported - explicitly acknowledged in Section 6: 'averaged across multiple execution runs... would be ideal for a more thorough characterization, and is planned as future work'. One required element (variance/repeated runs) is missing for the main evaluation.
column174: Both required aspects are explicitly discussed. Scope/failure modes: Section 6 Limitations ('The design principles target systems with static or sporadically changing structures'; 'Component-based modeling introduces some rigidity: behaviors not expressible through existing library components require extension'), plus failure-mode analysis in Sections 5.4-5.5 (hierarchy collapse, positional-reasoning failures, irregular structures being disproportionately error-prone). Threats to validity of the evaluation itself: 'all experiments used a single LLM backend (Gemini 2.5 Pro). Comparative analysis across multiple LLM models, averaged across multiple execution runs... would be ideal' and 'The study applies specifically to manufacturing systems representable within FactorySimPy's component scope; generalizability to other simulation domains remains to be studied' (Section 6).
column176: Explicit conceptual differentiation from named prior solutions, per solution: monolithic LLM code generation ('When LLMs generate monolithic simulation code directly (for example, [3, 20, 13])... FactoryFlow constrains model generation to instantiating and interconnecting validated components from the FactorySimPy library', Section 4 Principle 2); schema/enumerative IRs ('Schema-based representations including CMSD, XML, and JSON provide standardized formats for manufacturing simulation [27, 21], though their instance-oriented nature limits scalability for large, regular structures', Section 2); joint structure-parameter inference ('Several data-driven AMG methods infer structure and parameters jointly from a single source... Binding the two into a single automation step forces a compromise', Section 4 Principle 1). The error taxonomy is also positioned against a named prior taxonomy [34] ('Our eight-category taxonomy is consistent with this finding in the DES modeling setting', Section 2). Differentiation is conceptual per approach rather than an empirical head-to-head against external systems (the netlist baseline is the authors' own prior prototype), but this meets the criterion of explicit differentiation from named prior solutions.
column183: Model version: a single LLM is used and named exactly - 'We use Gemini 2.5 Pro with few-shot prompting' (Section 3) and 'all experiments used a single LLM backend (Gemini 2.5 Pro)' (Section 6); this is a specific version identifier analogous to 'Llama 3.1 70B Instruct', though no dated snapshot is given -> true. Prompts: only the prompt assembly is described ('description, assumptions, and supporting materials (FactorySimPy API specification, example models, system prompt)', Section 3; 'System prompt' and 'Examples' boxes in Figure 1); no verbatim prompts appear in the paper, and the repository inventory (Section 5.1: 'benchmark model set, natural language descriptions, LLM-generated outputs, identified errors, and analysis scripts') does not explicitly list prompts -> partial. Decoding parameters: no temperature, top-p, max-token or seed values reported anywhere -> false. Code: 'FactoryFlow is an open-source, LLM-assisted framework' (Abstract, Section 3) with the GitHub repository cited ([8], [9], [10]) and contents 'publicly available in the FactoryFlow GitHub repository' (Section 5.1) -> true. Data: 'A comprehensive dataset documenting this characterization study including the benchmark model set, natural language descriptions, LLM-generated outputs, identified errors, and analysis scripts is publicly available in the FactoryFlow GitHub repository [8]' (Section 5.1) -> full. Run date: no date or period during which the LLM was queried is reported -> false.

column18: SceneGenAgent is a novel LLM-based coding agent evaluated in a controlled lab/benchmark setting rather than in operational practice. The authors construct a purpose-built benchmark of 40 industrial scene descriptions (Section 4.1) and evaluate pass@1 via manual expert inspection ('We rely on manual verification, carefully comparing each scene against its description', Section 4.1), supplemented by ablation studies (Section 4.3). Although the benchmark descriptions were written by 15 engineers and the work is in collaboration with Siemens, the technique itself is not yet deployed in practice — the evaluation is an artificial/controlled benchmark experiment, so this is validation-research rather than evaluation-research.
column20: A working system is fully implemented and publicly released ('Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/THUDM/SceneGenAgent', Section 1) and evaluated under a defined protocol with defined metrics: a 40-description benchmark across 5 categories, pass@1 estimated from 5 samples per description at temperature 1, and manual evaluation by a 3-member expert team proficient in Process Simulate (Section 4.1). Quantitative results are reported, e.g., GPT-4o achieving 81.0% overall pass@1 (Table 2) and fine-tuned Llama3.1-70B reaching 78.5%.
column21: Industrial manufacturing / digital manufacturing (Siemens Tecnomatix, Process Simulate)
column22: The paper explicitly targets industrial manufacturing: 'The modeling of industrial scenes is essential for simulations in industrial manufacturing' (Abstract), and the system leverages Tecnomatix, 'a dedicated digital manufacturing software developed by Siemens' (Section 1), with code executed in Process Simulate to render scenes (Section 2).
column23: Industrial scene generation — welding workstations / manufacturing cells (robots, work tables, conveyors, cabinets, guarding) generated from textual descriptions
column24: The evaluation domain is industrial scene layout generation: the benchmark (Section 4.1; full descriptions in Tables 6–8, Appendix A.9) consists entirely of descriptions of welding stations and industrial workstations involving robotic arms (KUKA, ABB, YASKAWA), welding tables, turntables, conveyors, cabinets, valve stands, and safety guarding, rendered in Siemens Process Simulate.
column26: No explicit research questions are stated in the paper. The work is instead motivated via a challenge statement (current LLMs struggle to meet the precision requirements of industrial scene generation, Section 1) and enumerates three contributions ('The contributions are summarized as follows...', Section 1). No RQ-style questions appear anywhere in the text.
column28: SceneGenAgent generates layouts of industrial production workstations: it retrieves objects (robotic arms, welding tables, turntables, conveyors, cabinets, valve stands, guarding) from an object library and assigns their exact placements (millimeter coordinates and orientations), rendering the scene in Siemens Tecnomatix Process Simulate (Abstract; §1; §2; §3.1; Appendix A.5.1). This is facility/workstation layout planning within a factory, mapping to the factory-planning subdomain per Appendix A. No SC-network, logistics/distribution-network, technology-selection, site-selection, or GPN content is present.
column31: Core task factory-layout-planning: the agent 'performs layout analysis to recover the objects O and placements P' and 'assigns the final placement of every object' (§3.1.1), i.e., it plans the spatial layout of industrial workstations from textual descriptions ('precise layout planning', Abstract). Secondary task simulation-modeling: the method generates C# code that is 'run in the Process Simulate software to render the scene' (§2), creating digital scene models in Siemens Tecnomatix; the authors state 'The modeling of industrial scenes is essential for simulations in industrial manufacturing' (Abstract) and that generated digital models serve 'design visualization, simulation, analysis, and optimization in manufacturing' (§1), with the object library used 'for modeling and simulating workstations with different layouts' (Appendix A.5.1).
column33: The decision concerns the arrangement of production equipment (robots, work tables, conveyors, safety guarding) in manufacturing workstations (§1; §3.1; benchmark descriptions in Appendix A.9), i.e., the production process of the SCP Matrix. No procurement, distribution, or sales decisions are addressed.
column35: The method determines exact object placements - coordinates in millimeters and orientations - for industrial workstations (§2; §3.1.1), corresponding to detailed layout planning (VDI 5200 Phase 4, Detailplanung). The paper does not cite VDI 5200; the mapping is by task granularity, driven by the paper's emphasis on 'quantitative measurements and precise positioning' (§1). ? The method could also aid Phase 3 concept planning (rapid layout/design visualization, incl. fuzzy descriptions, §1; §4.1), but the demonstrated decision output is the precise, detailed layout, so only Phase 4 is coded.
column37: No time horizon (e.g., a number of years) is stated anywhere in the paper (searched Abstract, §1, §3, §4, §6); the task is scene/layout generation with no temporal planning scope.
column40: No horizon statements appear in the paper (cf. time_horizon fields). The supported decision - the workstation layout: which equipment is placed at which exact positions/orientations - configures the system (determines what exists in the planned scene/cell) rather than allocating or scheduling existing resources over time; per the schema rule, Strategic is selected iff system_configuring_decision is true, which holds here ('assigns the final placement of every object', §3.1.1; 'precise layout planning', Abstract). No tactical (mid-term resource allocation) or operational (short-term scheduling/control) decisions are produced or supported.

(The phrase 'operational efficiency' in a data example, Appendix A.3, refers to workspace efficiency, not a planning tier.)

(§1 Introduction). Also: 'SceneGenAgent ensures precise layout planning through a structured and calculable format, layout verification, and iterative refinement...' (Abstract). column49: No planning-domain framework (VDI 5200, SC Planning Matrix, Wiendahl-Nyhuis, Lanza et al. 2019, Melo et al. 2009, or another planning reference model) is cited or used to structure the planning scope. The paper is framed as an LLM-based coding/scene-generation agent; related work covers LLM and 3D scene generation systems (LayoutGPT, 3D-GPT, Holodeck, SceneCraft, GALA3D, LLMR) (§5) and methods like Evol-Instruct and LoRA (§3.2) - none of which structure a planning scope.
column50: The paper structures its scope around LLM agent design (layout analysis pipeline, code generation with Tecnomatix APIs) and the scene-generation literature, not around any factory or supply chain planning reference model; no planning-domain framework is invoked anywhere in the text (§1, §3, §5).
column52: SceneGenAgent is an LLM-based agent that generates precise industrial scenes from textual descriptions by producing C# code that is executed in Siemens Tecnomatix Process Simulate. Input: natural-language industrial scene descriptions with quantitative constraints (coordinates, distances, orientations, object quantities). The agent pipeline: (1) object retrieval – an LLM identifies objects in the description and maps them to a predefined object library, rewriting the description; (2) layout extraction – an LLM extracts positions and relations into a structured, calculable format; (3) placement assignment – an LLM converts relations into coordinate differences, computes coordinates and directions, and allocates placements satisfying constraints (e.g., ≥1 m inter-object distance); (4) verification – an LLM iteratively checks the placement for description violations and collisions, feeding detected errors back to refine the placement until error-free; (5) code generation – an LLM writes C# code using Tecnomatix APIs, guided by a code template and coding guidance, with rule-based API-usage checks and revision. The generated code is run to render the 3D industrial scene for design visualization and simulation in manufacturing. Open-source LLMs can be fine-tuned on the SceneInstruct dataset to enable independent deployment.
column54: Deployed and evaluated with SceneGenAgent (Table 2, §4.1): API-based GPT-4o and GLM-4-Plus complete all agent operations; open-source chat models Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Llama3.1-8B, GLM4-9B, Codestral-22B, CodeLlama-34B and Llama3.1-70B (§3.2.2) are fine-tuned on SceneInstruct and evaluated during placement assignment, with Llama3.1-70B also evaluated without fine-tuning (Tables 2–3) and handling the non-assignment operations for the smaller open models (§4.1). Other LLMs appear only outside the evaluated system: GPT-4 assigns placement during SceneInstruct trajectory collection (§3.2.1); Llama3.1-70B additionally performs Evol-Instruct description rewriting and stage selection for data collection (§3.2.1, Appendix A.4.1); Llama3.1-8B generates extra error-containing placement data (§3.2.1). Holodeck's placement module is used in an ablation comparison (Appendix A.1), not as an LLM backbone.
column55: API-based LLMs (GPT-4o, GLM-4-Plus) handle all agent operations when used as the backbone (§4.1). Open-source LLMs are applied only during placement assignment while Llama3.1-70B manages the remaining operations, because SceneInstruct covers only the placement-assignment stage and smaller models struggle in the other operations (§4.1, Appendix A.5.2). Fine-tuned Llama3.1-70B approaches GPT-4o (78.5% vs 81.0% overall pass@1, Table 2). In dataset construction, GPT-4 assigns placement for base trajectories, Llama3.1-8B for extra error data, and Llama3.1-70B rewrites descriptions and completes tasks up to layout extraction (§3.2.1).
column57: GPT-4o is OpenAI GPT family (§4.1). GLM-4-Plus and GLM4-9B are Zhipu AI GLM family (§3.2.2, §4.1). Qwen2.5-Coder-7B is Alibaba Qwen family (§3.2.2). Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.1-70B and CodeLlama-34B are Meta Llama family (§3.2.2). Codestral-22B is Mistral AI's code model, i.e., Mistral family (§3.2.2).
column60: Mixed (Table 2 'Type' column, §4.1): open-weight models are Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Llama3.1-8B, GLM4-9B, Codestral-22B, CodeLlama-34B and Llama3.1-70B – the paper calls them 'open-source LLMs' and fine-tunes them with LoRA (§3.2.2). Proprietary: GPT-4o (OpenAI API) and GLM-4-Plus (Zhipu API tier, coded 'closed' in Table 2) – weights not openly available.
column63: Mixed: GPT-4o and GLM-4-Plus are 'API-based LLMs' (§4.1; Table 2 'closed'), accessed via provider APIs. The open-source models are fine-tuned with LoRA (which requires local weights) and the approach is motivated by 'allowing individuals to deploy it independently' (§1), implying local/on-prem hosting; GPU compute was sponsored by Zhipu AI (Acknowledgments). The exact inference infrastructure for the open models during evaluation is not explicitly stated (?), but LoRA fine-tuning and the independent-deployment framing indicate local execution.
column65: Text: the LLM receives textual scene descriptions, object-library lists, and positions/relations serialized as JSON/text, and outputs structured text and C# code (§3.1, Appendix A.7). No images or other modalities are fed to the LLM in the method; scene rendering in Process Simulate and manual visual evaluation happen outside the LLM (§4.1, Appendix A.5.2). Multimodal LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o vision) were explored only for automated evaluation and found unsuitable (Appendix A.5.2) – not part of the method.
column67: LoRA: 'we utilize LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), fine-tune multiple LoRA modules corresponding to tasks, and dynamically switch modules in deployment' (§3.2.2); LoRA rank 64, alpha 128 (Table 5). Applied only to the six open-source models; the API-based GPT-4o and GLM-4-Plus are not fine-tuned. The objective is supervised instruction tuning on SceneInstruct trajectories (not coded separately per schema note).
column68: Six open-source chat models (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Llama3.1-8B, GLM4-9B, Codestral-22B, CodeLlama-34B, Llama3.1-70B) are fine-tuned on SceneInstruct using LoRA, with multiple task-specific LoRA modules (assign, verify, reassign placement) dynamically switched in deployment (§3.2.2). SceneInstruct contains 21,756 instances (20,688 train / 1,068 validation; Table 1, Appendix A.2.2) built from 3,002 industrial scene descriptions synthesized by Evol-Instruct rewriting of 20 hand-written descriptions with Llama3.1-70B; trajectories were collected with GPT-4 assigning placement (base data) and Llama3.1-8B for extra error data (§3.2.1). Assignment/verification data are organized as question-answer pairs and reassignment data as conversations; loss is computed on outputs in the final rounds (§3.2.2). Hyperparameters per model in Table 5 (peak LR 1e-5 to 1e-4, batch size 64–256, LoRA rank 64, alpha 128, 2–8 epochs).
column71: zero-shot: the layout-analysis prompts (object retrieval, layout extraction, placement assignment, verification) provide instructions and output formats without worked task examples (Appendix A.7.1). CoT: prompts require explicit analysis/calculation before the final answer – 'You should first perform calculations to get the coordinates in the analysis part, then come up with the final positions' – and outputs include 'Analysis:' sections (§3.1.1, Appendix A.7.1, A.3). structured-output: outputs are constrained to fixed formats and JSON schemas (e.g., Positions/Relative Positions JSON lists, fixed step-by-step return formats; Appendix A.7.1). few-shot: code generation is guided by a code template plus 'usage guidelines and example code snippets corresponding to APIs' (§3.1.2, Appendix A.7.1) – in-context code examples the model must 'strictly follow', though these are API-usage snippets rather than full input/output pairs (?).
column74: Although the paper calls SceneGenAgent an 'LLM-based agent' (§1, §3.1), the workflow is a fixed, developer-defined sequence of specialised LLM roles – object retrieval → layout extraction → placement assignment → verification/refinement loop → code generation → rule-based check → execution (§3.1, Figure 2). No LLM component decides its next action or tool call at run time; the control flow is fixed by the developer. Per the schema definition this is a pipeline, not a single-/multi-agent system.
column76: prompt-chaining: fixed sequence of LLM calls, each processing the previous output – object retrieval rewrites the description s; layout extraction produces positions P and relations R from s; placement assignment computes placement P from P and R; code generation writes C# code from P (§3.1.1–3.1.2). evaluator-optimizer: placement assignment (generator LLM) produces P; a separate verification LLM call ('Check placement' prompt, Appendix A.7.1/A.3) checks P for constraint violations and collisions and returns errors; the errors are fed back ('Placement Error Feedback' prompt) to reassign placement 'until no errors are found' (§3.1.1 Verification). The code-generation check is rule-based keyword scanning (§3.1.2) – deterministic feedback, not an LLM evaluator – so it does not count as evaluator-optimizer per schema.
column80: agent_memory = short-term: within one scene-generation task the agent carries intermediate artifacts (rewritten description, object list, extracted positions/relations, current placement, detected errors) across successive LLM calls; the verification–refinement loop feeds the previous placement and the LLM-generated error critique back into reassignment, and reassignment data is organized as multi-turn conversations (§3.2.2, Appendix A.3). No long-term/persistent memory across tasks is described. Note: state is passed via prompts assembled by the fixed pipeline rather than via an explicit memory module – borderline interpretation flagged. planning_reflection = true: the verification stage is an explicit LLM self-critique ('Recent studies … have shown the ability of language models to critique their own decisions. Hence, SceneGenAgent iteratively checks P …', §3.1.1), with detected errors used as feedback to refine the placement before code generation; placement assignment also performs explicit step-wise planning (infer coordinate differences, compute coordinates, allocate placement, §3.1.1). tool_use = false: all LLM calls occur at developer-fixed positions in the pipeline; the LLM generates C# code but does not itself decide at run time which tools/functions to call; code execution and the rule-based API check are developer-fixed steps (§3.1).
column82: code-execution: SceneGenAgent generates C# code that is executed – 'The code is run in the Process Simulate software to render the scene' (§2); 'Once the code passes the check, we run it to render the industrial scene' (§3.1.2). simulation-platform: the executed code uses Tecnomatix APIs and runs in Siemens Tecnomatix Process Simulate, a dedicated digital manufacturing/simulation software, to render the 3D industrial scene (§1, §2, §3.1.2). The object library (from the Process Simulate tutorial, Appendix A.5.1) is supplied as text within prompts, not retrieved via an external system. No RAG, solver, ML-model, digital-twin, database-SQL, enterprise-system, CAD-GIS or web-search integration is part of the method.
column84: SceneGenAgent (§3.1, Figure 2) generates industrial scene layouts through LLM-based reasoning: object retrieval, layout extraction (positions/relations), placement assignment via computed coordinate differences, and iterative LLM self-verification/refinement. This is a generate-verify-refine loop performed by the LLM's own reasoning, which per the schema is not an optimization tradition. No mathematical program, solver call, metaheuristic, RL search, MCDM ranking, or simulation-optimization is formulated or invoked by the proposed method. 'Optimization' appears only as a downstream use of generated scenes (§1: 'design visualization, simulation, analysis, and optimization in manufacturing') and in related work (§5: SceneCraft's learnable scoring functions, GALA3D), not in the method itself.
column86: No optimization tradition is present, so formalization is 'none'. The placement assignment (§3.1.1) uses a structured, calculable format for positions and relations and checks constraints (Euclidean distance ≥ 1 m, collision avoidance, description compliance), but there is no formal objective function or optimization model—only LLM-computed constraint satisfaction and refinement.
column88: No optimization paradigm applies because the method performs no optimization of its own; placements are computed by LLM reasoning over coordinate differences and constraints (§3.1.1), not by any solver, search algorithm, or scoring/optimization procedure.
column91: Since no optimizer exists in the method, the LLM's role relative to an optimizer is 'none'. The LLM serves as a scene-layout planner and C# code generator (§3.1); its verification step (§3.1.1) is self-critique within its own generate-improve loop rather than interaction with an external optimizer.
column93: No optimization solver is used or mentioned. The generated C# code runs in Siemens Tecnomatix Process Simulate (§2, §3.1.2) to render scenes; this is digital-manufacturing rendering software, not an optimization solver. NR.
column96: The paper's own method is evaluated on an author-built benchmark of 40 industrial scene descriptions, scored via pass@1 against the descriptions through manual expert inspection (§4.1 'Benchmark' and 'Metric and evaluation'; main results in §4.2 Table 2) — test-set. Additionally, controlled condition comparisons are run on the same benchmark/tasks: with vs. without the agent workflow, with vs. without verification (§4.3.1, Table 3), with vs. without Tecnomatix API guidance (§4.3.2), and across training-data proportions 10/20/50/90/100% (§4.3.3, Figure 4) — quasi-experimental. No user study, single/multi-case, or field deployment is reported.
column98: The evaluation addresses a real problem of a real organisation (industrial scene generation for manufacturing simulation, in collaboration with Siemens Ltd.) on that organisation's own system (Siemens Tecnomatix Process Simulate, in which the generated C# code is executed to render scenes; §2, §3.1.2), and involves real users: the 40 benchmark descriptions were written by 15 engineers based on their experience, with category proportions reflecting real-world frequency of occurrence (§4.1), and outputs are judged by a 3-member expert team with industrial-scene and Process Simulate proficiency (§4.1 'Metric and evaluation'). The paper frames the tasks as 'real-world industrial scene generation tasks' (Abstract). Per schema, expert-constructed requirement statements do not make such an episode artificial. ? Caveat: the benchmark items were purpose-built for evaluation rather than drawn from live production data, so a stricter 'test set = artificial' reading is arguable.

column139: The dedicated 'Limitations' section states these two limitations: 'Broader applications' (experiments focus on industrial contexts; expansion to generalized scene generation is planned future work) and 'Evaluation methods' (manual evaluation is labor-intensive and susceptible to subjective bias; future work could develop automated evaluation methods).
column140: SceneGenAgent substantially improves LLM performance on industrial scene generation: GPT-4o with the agent reaches 81.0% overall pass@1 on the 40-description benchmark (GLM-4-Plus 73.5%), which the authors report as effectively meeting most scene generation requirements. Ablations show the agent workflow and verification are critical: removing the agent drops GPT-4o to 73.5% (-9.3%), GLM-4-Plus to 49.5% (-32.7%), and Llama3.1-70B to 48.5% (-33.6%); removing verification also degrades all models. Fine-tuning open-source LLMs on SceneInstruct yields consistent gains across scales, with Llama3.1-70B rising from 73.0% to 78.5%, approaching GPT-4o. Replacing SceneGenAgent's layout analysis with Holodeck's placement planning drops pass@1 from 73.0% to 28.0%, and removing Tecnomatix API guidance yields 0% (all code fails to compile). Data-scaling experiments indicate a critical threshold of training data is required for generalization, with performance fluctuating below the untrained baseline up to 50% of data and moderately increasing at 90%.
column143: False. The SceneGenAgent workflow contains no human acting on intermediate or final LLM output. Layout verification and refinement are performed by the LLM itself (§3.1.1: 'the agent uses P, R, P, and the detected errors as input and attempts to fix the errors to generate a new P until no errors are found'), and code checking is rule-based (§3.1.2: 'The agent conducts a rule-based evaluation by scanning keywords associated with the APIs in the code'). The 3-member expert evaluation team (§4.1) only inspects already-rendered final scenes to compute pass@1 for the benchmark, i.e., reading the final answer for post hoc scoring, which does not count as HITL. Human-written descriptions (§3.2.1, Appendix A.9) are dataset/benchmark construction, not workflow steps.
column149: True. Domain knowledge is encoded in explicit, reusable, machine-readable structures the system uses: (1) a C# code template encoding the Tecnomatix API scene-modeling structure that the agent fills in (§3.1.2: 'We design a code template containing basic code, such as initialization, and leave the parts responsible for model loading and object placement incomplete for the agent to fill'), accompanied by API coding guidance with 'usage guidelines and example code snippets corresponding to APIs'; (2) a structured, calculable format for spatial specifications — positions p=(oi,li,di) and relations r=(oi,oj,rij) (§3.1.1: 'representing spatial specifications including positions and relations in a structured, calculable format') — with predefined JSON output schemas the LLM must conform to (Appendix A.7.1, e.g., 'Positions: [ { "name": "<name>", "position": "[x, y, 0]", "orientation": "<orientation>" } ]').
column151: code-template: §3.1.2 'We design a code template containing basic code... leave the parts responsible for model loading and object placement incomplete for the agent to fill'; the code-generation prompt (Appendix A.7.1) supplies a full C# skeleton with Tecnomatix API calls (TxInsertComponentCreationData, TxTransformation, etc.) that the LLM adapts and completes. structured-schema: §3.1.1 formalizes layout as sets of positions P and relations R in 'a structured, calculable format', and the prompts (Appendix A.7.1) enforce predefined JSON schemas for objects, positions, relative positions, and placements that LLM outputs must match. No ontology/knowledge graph, standards encoding, relational database, or formal optimization/simulation model is reported; the Tecnomatix object library (20 models of 10 types, Appendix A.5.1) is a 3D-asset collection used for retrieval, not a formalized entity schema, so relational-database is not coded.
column152: The system formalizes industrial scene structure in two ways. First, a C# code template encoding the Tecnomatix API structure for scene modeling (initialization, loading models from the Welding library, inserting components and setting coordinates/orientations via TxInsertComponentCreationData and TxTransformation) that the agent completes, supported by coding guidance with API usage guidelines and example code snippets (§3.1.2, Appendix A.7.1). Second, a structured, calculable layout representation: objects characterized by 2D coordinates and directions, positions p=(oi,li,di) and pairwise relations r=(oi,oj,rij) that are rewritten into coordinate differences for computation, with LLM outputs conforming to predefined JSON schemas for positions, relations, and placements, plus constraints such as Euclidean distance >= 1 meter to avoid collision (§2, §3.1.1, Appendix A.7.1). An object library of 20 models of 10 industrial types (robots, welding tables, turntables, conveyors, cabinets, valve stands, guarding) from the Siemens Tecnomatix Process Simulate tutorial is used for object retrieval (Appendix A.5.1).
column155: True. §4.1 ('Benchmark', 'Metric and evaluation') defines an explicit, repeatable protocol: a test instrument of 40 industrial scene descriptions written by 15 engineers and split into 5 categories (geometric arrangement, positional details, object quantity, composite description, fuzzy description); a defined metric (pass@1 with estimator pass@k = E[1 - (n-c k)/(nk)], 5 samples per description at temperature t=1); and a stated procedure (manual verification by a 3-member expert team proficient in Process Simulate, with each evaluator reviewing at least one of the five samples per description to mitigate subjectivity). Full benchmark items are listed in Appendix A.9.
column157: custom-test-set: §4.1 'We develop a comprehensive industrial scene layout generation benchmark containing 40 descriptions of industrial scenes. These descriptions are written by 15 engineers based on their experience' — a test set built by the authors for this paper, not a public benchmark reused from prior work, so 'benchmark' is not coded. expert-ground-truth: §4.1 'Our evaluation team consists of 3 members with expertise in industrial scenes and proficiency in the Process Simulate software... carefully comparing each scene against its description' — output correctness is judged by domain experts. pass@1 is a generic code-generation metric (Chen et al., 2021), not a domain-defined metric, and scoring is binary pass/fail rather than a graded scale, so domain-specific-metric and rubric are not coded.
column158: A 40-description industrial scene generation benchmark authored by 15 engineers, covering 5 categories (geometric arrangement, positional details, object quantity, composite description, fuzzy description) with proportions reflecting real-world occurrence frequency (§4.1, Appendix A.9, Tables 6-8). Each description is sampled 5 times at temperature t=1, and pass@1 is computed with the estimator pass@k = E[1 - (n-c k)/(nk)] with n=5, k=1. Because no automated testing tool suite exists for the industrial software, correctness is verified manually: 3 evaluators with industrial-scene expertise and Process Simulate proficiency compare each rendered scene against its description, and each evaluator reviews at least one of the five samples per description to minimize subjectivity bias. Results are reported overall and per category, with ablations (w/o agent, w/o verification, w/o API guidance, data scaling, Holodeck placement planning comparison) in Tables 2-4 and Figure 4.
column166: information-acquisition: §3.1.1 Object retrieval — 'SceneGenAgent identifies the objects in the scene and retrieves the corresponding items from the object library', mapping description objects to library assets at run time (retrieval over an external model library beyond the given description). information-analysis: §3.1.1 Layout extraction and placement assignment — extracting positions and relations from the description and 'computing and reasoning with numerical constraints' to infer coordinates and directions. decision-selection: §3.1.1 Verification — the system actively evaluates the placement against description constraints and collisions and refines it, producing the single final layout plan ('attempts to fix the errors to generate a new P until no errors are found'); no human ranks alternatives. action-implementation: §3.1.2 and §1 — the system writes the selected layout into C# code using Tecnomatix APIs and executes it itself: 'executes the code to render the corresponding scene' / 'Once the code passes the check, we run it to render the industrial scene' in Process Simulate.
column168: 4-autonomous. Given a scene description, SceneGenAgent autonomously determines the complete final object placement (initial assignment, self-verification and iterative refinement all performed by the LLM agent, §3.1.1) and implements it by generating C# code that is executed to render the scene in Process Simulate (§1: 'SceneGenAgent translates scene descriptions into C# code... and executes the code to render the corresponding scene'; §3.1.2: 'Once the code passes the check, we run it to render the industrial scene'). There is no human approval, veto, or option-selection step anywhere in the workflow; human experts only evaluate rendered scenes post hoc for benchmark scoring (§4.1), which does not constrain the decision.
column170: Architecture, prompts, models, data sources and key parameters are all available. The pipeline is fully specified (Section 3, Figure 2: object retrieval, layout extraction, placement assignment with iterative verification, then C# code generation against Tecnomatix APIs). All prompts are given verbatim in Appendix A.7 (Object Retrieval, Layout Extraction, Placement Assignment, Placement Verification, Placement Error Feedback, Code Generation, plus the two ablation prompts), with worked input/output examples in A.3. Models are named (Section 4.1: GPT-4o, GLM-4-Plus, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Llama3.1-8B, GLM4-9B, Codestral-22B, CodeLlama-34B, Llama3.1-70B). Knowledge/data sources are specified: the object library is 'from the Siemens Tecnomatix Process Simulate tutorial, containing 20 different models of 10 types' (A.5.1), and SceneInstruct construction is detailed (Section 3.2.1, A.4). Key parameters are reported: sampling 'with temperature t = 1' and 5 samples (Section 4.1) plus training hyper-parameters in Table 5 (A.6). Code and dataset are released: 'Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/THUDM/SceneGenAgent.'
column172: Category A (implemented and validated on a real-world benchmark). The metric is operationally defined with its estimator and procedure: 'we sample 5 times for each description with temperature t = 1 and evaluate pass@1 with the estimator pass@k = E[1 - (n-c k )/(nk)], where n is the number of samples for each problem (5 in this work)' (Section 4.1), scored by manual verification from '3 members with expertise in industrial scenes' with a bias-mitigation protocol (each evaluator reviews at least one of the five samples). Sample size (40-description benchmark, Section 4.1/A.9), repeated runs (5 samples per description), and comparators are all reported: multiple LLMs (Table 2), ablations 'w/o agent' and 'w/o verification' (Table 3), and an empirical comparison against Holodeck's placement planning (Table 4). Reported results support the text's claims (e.g., GPT-4o 81.0% overall pass@1 in Table 2 matches the abstract's 'reaching up to 81.0% success rate').
column174: The Limitations section covers both scope ('Our experiments predominantly focus on object assets and textual descriptions within industrial contexts... We plan to expand this work to more generalized scene generation') and threats to the validity of the evaluation itself ('our evaluation relies on manual evaluation, which is labor-intensive and inherently susceptible to subjective bias'). Further evaluation-validity discussion appears in A.5.2 (CLIP scores are 'insufficient to evaluate a scene's quantitative accuracy'; multimodal LLMs 'struggle to extract precise quantitative information from images, making them unsuitable for evaluation'). Failure modes are also analyzed, e.g., 'All generated code fails to compile without API guidance' (Section 4.3.2) and limited-data generalization effects (Section 4.3.3).
column176: Section 5 explicitly differentiates the contribution from named prior solutions per solution: LayoutGPT/3D-GPT/SceneX 'directly generate configurations of the scene'; LLMR 'relies on validation to refine the LLM's layout planning'; SceneCraft models constraints with 'learnable scoring functions'; Holodeck 'employs depth-first search on a relational constraint graph'; GALA3D uses '3D Gaussian splatting representations' — concluding 'SceneGenAgent differentiates from them by regarding layout information as computable and refinable data structures, enabling precise placement through calculation and reasoning.' This is supplemented by an empirical head-to-head: Appendix A.1 integrates Holodeck's placement planning into the same framework and shows the original SceneGenAgent 'substantially outperforms the version employing Holodeck's placement planning module' (Table 4: 73.0 vs 28.0 overall pass@1).
