column18: The paper proposes a novel LLM-driven, multi-tool risk assessment pipeline and evaluates it on a researcher-controlled testbed rather than in operational practice. Section 3 states 'We use Georgia as the testbed in this study', and Section 5 (Case Study) runs the implemented system (ReAct-based agent on LangGraph with ChatOpenAI gpt-4o, per Section 4) on Georgia logistic hubs using public data sources (BTS/FAF hub data, NOAA storm records, traffic status, news, Wikipedia), producing daily 2024 risk assessments, yearly summaries, cosine-similarity and clustering analyses. No real organization uses the system in operational use, and the data is public/governmental rather than real company data, so this does not meet evaluation-research; it is a novel technique evaluated on test cases in an artificial setting, i.e., validation-research. It goes beyond solution-proposal because a full case study (not merely a small example) is conducted, including a two-step assessment protocol and full-year daily assessments.
column20: A working system is implemented and demonstrated: Section 4 describes 'a ReAct-based framework... leveraging the LangGraph platform... Using ChatOpenAI with the gpt-4o model', integrating seven external tools (hub data, Wikipedia, finance, NOAA storm data, news aggregation, traffic status, notebook). Section 5 demonstrates it on the Georgia case study with example outputs (Figure 3), a risk-based cosine-similarity heatmap, and hub clustering (Figure 4). However, no evaluation protocol with defined performance metrics is reported: there is no ground-truth comparison, benchmark, accuracy/precision/recall of risk identification, or user study; cosine similarity is a method component for clustering rather than a system-performance metric. Per the decision rules (working system demonstrated on a case without defined metrics), validation_status = 'prototype'.
column21: Logistics / supply chain (hyperconnected logistic hub networks, Physical Internet)
column22: The Abstract and Section 1 frame the work around 'the deployment of hyperconnected logistic hub networks' and 'global supply chains', including open freight flow consolidation and Physical Internet-based networks; Section 3 specifies risk assessment for 'logistics hubs proposed for a Physical Internet based hyperconnected logistic network'. The industry sector is therefore logistics/supply chain.
column23: Risk assessment for logistic hub deployment in a Physical Internet-based hyperconnected logistic network, using the U.S. state of Georgia as the testbed (hubs derived from the BTS Freight Analysis Framework database)
column24: Section 3 (Problem Definition): 'we conduct risk assessment for logistics hubs proposed for a Physical Internet based hyperconnected logistic network... designed based on data extracted from Freight Analysis Framework (FAF) database produced by the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS)... We use Georgia as the testbed in this study.' Section 5 applies the pipeline to Georgia hubs, identifying risk types (thunderstorm winds, tornadoes, flash floods, lightning, floods, hail, strong winds, traffic jams) and clustering hubs by risk profile (Figure 4).
column25: No formal research questions are stated. Closest paraphrase of the stated research aim (Section 3): assuming all hubs are deployed, leverage LLMs and external tools to (1) analyze structured and unstructured data, (2) identify risk types, (3) conduct daily risk assessments aggregated into yearly summaries, and (4) cluster logistic hubs based on their risk profiles to uncover regional risk patterns and support strategic decision-making in logistic hub deployment.
column26: The paper contains no explicit 'RQ1/RQ2' statements. The closest is the aim summary in Section 3: 'this research aims to leverage large language models (LLMs) and external tools to analyze both structured and unstructured data, identify risk types, conduct daily risk assessments and aggregate them into yearly summaries, and cluster logistic hubs based on their risk profiles to uncover regional risk patterns and support strategic decision-making in logistic hub deployment.' Extracted as a close paraphrase with the caveat that these are stated aims rather than formally numbered research questions.
column28: The paper performs LLM-driven risk assessment to support deployment of logistic hubs in a Physical Internet based hyperconnected logistic hub network (Abstract; §3). Tasks map to two subdomains: (1) logistics-distribution-network-design — the planning object is a strategic logistics/distribution hub network ('hyperconnected logistics hub networks', §1; 'deployment of logistic hub networks in global supply chains', §3); (2) site-selection — the method yields 'feasibility classifications, and explanations for hub placement decisions' (§4) and assesses 'the feasibility of hub selection' (Abstract), i.e., facility location. Not factory planning, technology selection, or GPN design; no supplier/plant/production network decisions are addressed, so SC-network-design is not used.
column31: facility-location: the framework 'produces detailed risk assessments, feasibility classifications, and explanations for hub placement decisions' (§4) and prompts instruct LLMs to assess 'the feasibility of hub selection' (Abstract) — deciding which hubs to deploy and where. logistics-distribution-network-planning: the decision concerns deployment of hubs as nodes of the downstream logistics/distribution network ('the design and deployment of logistic hub networks', §1; 'logistic hub deployment in hyperconnected supply chain networks', Abstract). resilience-risk-scenario-planning: the core method is risk identification, daily risk assessment, risk-level evaluation and risk-based clustering for network configuration ('identify risk types, conduct daily risk assessments... and cluster logistic hubs based on their risk profiles', §3; 'resilience measures such as real-time weather monitoring, contingency planning', §5).
column33: The decision concerns the distribution process of the Supply Chain Planning Matrix: logistic hubs, freight flow consolidation, and the transport/distribution network ('open freight flow consolidation', 'logistic hub networks', §1; 'hyperconnected logistic hub network deployment', Abstract). No procurement, production, or sales processes are addressed; hence distribution only.
column35: The study is not factory planning — it addresses logistic hub network deployment (§1, §3), so no VDI 5200 phase applies; coded NA per D034.
column37: No planning horizon for the hub deployment decision is stated. The paper only specifies the risk-data evaluation window — 'daily risk assessments for each logistic hub in 2024... aggregated into a comprehensive yearly summary' (§5; also §3 'conduct daily risk assessments and aggregate them into yearly summaries') — and a generic benefit phrase 'guiding long-term strategic planning' (§5); neither constitutes an explicitly stated planning horizon (e.g., '5 years') for the deployment decision.
column40: Strategic: the method supports hub deployment/placement decisions that determine which hubs exist in the hyperconnected logistic network — a system-configuring decision (see system_configuring_decision). Verbatim: 'support strategic decision-making in logistic hub deployment' (§3); 'guiding long-term strategic planning' (§5). The daily risk assessments (§5) are intermediate analyses aggregated into yearly summaries that feed the strategic deployment decision; the method produces no standalone tactical or operational planning decision (real-time traffic/weather data are used as risk inputs for hub feasibility, §4, not for short-term scheduling or mid-term resource allocation).
column42: Authors explicitly apply the 'strategic' label to the decision/planning supported: 'support strategic decision-making in logistic hub deployment' (§3); 'guiding long-term strategic planning' (§5); 'This framework facilitates the strategic reconfiguration of hubs based on evolving risk assessments' (§5). No 'tactical' or 'operational' label is applied to any planning decision ('strategic nodes' in §1 is an adjective describing hubs, not a planning claim).
column44: The supported decision determines what exists in the system: which logistic hubs are deployed/selected and where. Verbatim anchors: 'assessing the feasibility of hub selection' (Abstract); 'The framework produces detailed risk assessments, feasibility classifications, and explanations for hub placement decisions' (§4); 'support strategic decision-making in logistic hub deployment' (§3). Hub placement/deployment creates network nodes (sites), configuring the network rather than merely operating existing resources.
column46: Authors frame the decision as designing/selecting/locating system elements: 'the design and deployment of logistic hub networks' (§1); 'assessing the feasibility of hub selection' (Abstract); 'explanations for hub placement decisions' (§4). These statements say the decision designs, deploys, selects or locates hubs (facilities) in the network.
column47: The decision determines which logistic hubs are deployed/selected and their placement within the hyperconnected logistic hub network: the framework produces risk assessments, feasibility classifications, and explanations for hub placement/deployment decisions (Abstract; §3; §4), and risk-based clusters guide deployment, mitigation and network reconfiguration (§5).
column49: No planning-domain framework (VDI 5200, SC Planning Matrix, Lanza et al., Wiendahl-Nyhuis, Melo et al.) structures the paper's planning scope. The paper cites the Physical Internet concept as the application domain ('a Physical Internet based hyperconnected logistic network', §3) and the ReAct framework [22] for LLM agent implementation ('a ReAct-based [22] framework... leveraging the LangGraph platform', §4); ReAct is a general LLM reasoning-and-acting method, not a planning-domain reference model. Hence 'none'.
column50: The paper's approach is structured by an LLM-driven, tool-integrated agent pipeline (ReAct on LangGraph with gpt-4o, §4) and risk-based similarity/clustering analysis (cosine similarity, §5) — general AI/data methods, not planning-domain frameworks. The Physical Internet references define the application domain (the network paradigm), not a planning methodology structuring the deployment decision. No planning-domain reference model is used to structure the planning scope.
column52: The paper deploys an LLM-driven risk assessment pipeline for hyperconnected logistic hub network deployment. A central ReAct agent (GPT-4o via ChatOpenAI on the LangGraph platform) receives user directives (e.g., analyze risks for logistic hubs over specified time intervals) and dynamically invokes a toolkit of analytical tools: a Hub Information Extraction Tool (structured hub attributes from FAF-derived hub data), a Wikipedia Summary and Source Tool (geopolitical/cultural/environmental context), a Financial Data Analysis Tool (economic trends and stability; Yahoo Finance per Figure 2), a NOAA Storm Data Tool (historical storm events with type, property damage, injuries, fatalities), a News Aggregation Tool (emerging risks from real-time news), and a Traffic Status Tool (real-time congestion data). A Notebook Tool manages LLM token limits, processes data in structured batches, and organizes results into final summaries, serving as long-term storage/memory. The system identifies risk types (e.g., thunderstorm wind, tornado, flash flood, lightning, flood, hail, strong wind, traffic jam), generates daily per-hub risk assessments aggregated into yearly summaries, produces feasibility classifications with explanations supporting hub placement decisions, and clusters hubs by cosine similarity of standardized risk profiles to reveal regional risk patterns. Case study testbed: logistic hubs in Georgia, with hub data from the BTS Freight Analysis Framework (FAF) database.
column54: Only GPT-4o is deployed and evaluated with the paper's own method. Section 4 states: 'Using ChatOpenAI with the gpt-4o model, we initialize a reasoning engine.' No other LLMs are deployed, compared, or used as baselines anywhere in the paper, and no alternative backbones are tested. The ReAct citation [22] (Yao et al.) is a method/framework reference, not a deployed model. No uncertainty or contradictions noted.
column55: GPT-4o is the sole model, serving as the central reasoning engine/agent for all tasks: prompt processing, dynamic tool invocation, risk-type identification, daily risk assessment, and synthesis of explanations and summaries.
column57: GPT-4o is an OpenAI GPT-family model. Section 4: 'Using ChatOpenAI with the gpt-4o model' (ChatOpenAI is LangChain's OpenAI chat/API integration, footnote 3). Classified as 'GPT' per the family taxonomy; no other model families appear in the method.
column60: GPT-4o is a proprietary OpenAI model accessed via the ChatOpenAI API integration (Section 4); its weights are not openly available, so open_weight = N.
column63: Section 4: 'Using ChatOpenAI with the gpt-4o model, we initialize a reasoning engine', with footnote 3 referencing LangChain's OpenAI chat API integration documentation. The model is accessed as a hosted provider API; no local/on-prem deployment is mentioned anywhere in the paper.
column65: The LLM receives text only: user prompts/directives and textual (serialized) tool outputs such as hub attributes, Wikipedia summaries, financial data, NOAA storm records, news updates, and traffic readings (Sections 4-5; Figure 3 shows a text response). No image, CAD, audio, or other non-text input to the LLM is described; the maps/heatmaps in the figures are human-facing visualizations, not LLM inputs.
column67: No fine-tuning, weight updates, or training procedure is described anywhere in the paper. The method uses the pre-trained GPT-4o via prompting (ReAct) and tool integration (Sections 1 and 4). Hence fine_tuning = ['none'].
column71: Section 4: 'we design and implement a ReAct-based [22] framework... leveraging the LangGraph platform to integrate reasoning and action', i.e., interleaved reasoning and tool actions (ReAct). The abstract/introduction additionally state 'we design prompts that instruct LLMs to leverage these tools', i.e., custom instruction prompts within the ReAct loop. No few-shot examples, self-consistency sampling, or explicitly schema-constrained output prompting is described (the structured response in Figure 3 is an example output, not a described output constraint), so only ReAct is coded.
column74: Section 4 describes a single central agent: 'These prompts are then processed by the central agent, which orchestrates multiple tools, memory, and reasoning capabilities to generate insights' and 'The agent dynamically invokes these tools based on user instructions and data requirements.' The system is explicitly 'ReAct-based' and built with LangGraph - one agent looping over reasoning and tool use, where the tools are non-LLM components rather than sub-agents. Multi-agent systems appear only as future work (Section 6: 'integrating a multi-agent system could enhance scalability and efficiency'), so they are not coded.
column76: Section 5: 'A structured two-step approach is implemented to assess risks associated with logistic hub deployment.' Step 1: the GPT-4o agent identifies risk types and selects the most effective tools (NOAA Storm Data, Wikipedia Summary and Source, Traffic Status). Step 2: the GPT-4o agent conducts daily per-hub risk assessments for 2024 'using the selected tools and top risk types' from Step 1, aggregated into yearly summaries. This is a developer-fixed sequence of LLM stages in which the second stage processes the first stage's output -> prompt-chaining (components: risk-type identification/tool-selection stage -> daily risk assessment stage, both powered by GPT-4o). No routing, no reported parallelization of LLM calls, no orchestrator-workers (the orchestrated tools are non-LLM components, not LLM workers), and no evaluator-optimizer loop are described. Within each stage, a single ReAct agent autonomously loops over tool calls.
column80: agent_memory = long-term: Section 4 states 'the Notebook Tool serves as long-term storage, ensuring scalability and consistency' and 'By leveraging long-term memory, the system can track evolving risk patterns and incorporate historical data into future assessments'; the abstract highlights 'scalability with long-term memory' and contribution 2 cites 'LLMs' long-term memory' for processing extensive datasets across regions and time periods. Short-term context is also mentioned ('The memory component retains short-term context within multi-turn interactions'), but persistent long-term memory is the defining, emphasized capability, so 'long-term' is selected. planning_reflection = false: the ReAct framework interleaves reasoning and actions, but no explicit planning phase, self-critique, or reflection on its own output before the next step (e.g., plan-and-execute, Reflexion) is described. tool_use = true: 'The agent dynamically invokes these tools based on user instructions and data requirements' (Section 4); tools are 'automatically called by LLMs' (abstract); the ReAct framework 'dynamically connects the language model's reasoning capabilities with external tools for efficient data retrieval and analysis' (Section 4).
column82: Section 4 and Figure 2 describe a toolkit of external data tools the agent calls: Wikipedia Summary and Source Tool, Financial Data Analysis Tool (Yahoo Finance per Figure 2), NOAA Storm Data Tool, News Aggregation Tool, and Traffic Status Tool (real-time congestion data) - all external web APIs/data services, coded as web-search-API. The Wikipedia tool retrieves via an external API rather than a local document/vector store, so it is coded web-search-API rather than RAG. The Hub Information Extraction Tool processes pre-extracted structured hub data (from the BTS FAF database, Section 3) via predefined extraction; the LLM does not generate SQL queries itself, so database-SQL does not apply. The Notebook Tool is an internal batching/summary/long-term-storage component, not an external integration. The cosine-similarity and hierarchical-clustering analysis (Section 5) operates on the agent's standardized risk-profile outputs and is not described as an external non-LLM component called by the LLM (the abstract attributes the clustering to the LLMs), so ML-model is not coded. No solver, digital twin, simulation platform, code execution, enterprise system, or CAD/GIS tool integration is described.
column84: The proposed method is an LLM-driven risk assessment pipeline (§4 Methodology, §5 Case Study): it identifies risk types via tool calls, generates daily risk assessments aggregated into yearly summaries, and groups hubs via cosine similarity and hierarchical clustering (§5, §6 Conclusion). No mathematical program (variables, objective, constraints), MCDM ranking against explicit weighted criteria, metaheuristic or RL search, simulation-optimization, or solver call is formulated or executed by the method itself. 'Optimizing hub placement' appears only as background motivation in §1 ('optimize hub placement and operations') and as decision-support output for human decision-makers; the framework itself outputs risk assessments, feasibility classifications, and cluster insights rather than solving an optimization problem. LLM reasoning over tool outputs (ReAct-style) is explicitly not optimization per the schema definition.
column86: Formalization level is 'none' because optimization_tradition_present is false. The method's outputs (risk types, severity levels, feasibility classifications, risk-based hub clusters) are produced by LLM reasoning and tool calls (§4, §5) with no formal objective, decision variables, or constraints stated anywhere in the paper.
column88: optimization_paradigm is empty because optimization_tradition_present is false. The analytical techniques actually used—cosine similarity on standardized risk profiles and hierarchical clustering (§5, §6)—are descriptive data-analysis methods, not optimization paradigms in the schema's sense; no MILP/LP, NLP, CP, stochastic/robust program, metaheuristic, RL, MCDM, or simulation-optimization is employed by the method.
column91: llm_or_role is ['none'] because optimization_tradition_present is false (per D075/D079). The LLM (gpt-4o via a ReAct-based LangGraph agent, §4) orchestrates external tools (Wikipedia, NOAA storm data, news aggregation, traffic status, financial data, hub data) to assess risks and generate explanations and feasibility classifications, but there is no optimizer in the method for the LLM to formulate for, orchestrate, or interpret. The LLM's tool-calling serves data retrieval and risk analysis, not invocation of any optimization solver or model.
column93: No optimization solver is reported anywhere in the paper. The implementation uses LangGraph with ChatOpenAI (gpt-4o) as the reasoning engine (§4 Methodology); the external tools are data sources (Wikipedia, NOAA, news, traffic, finance, hub database) plus a Notebook tool for token-limit management, none of which is an optimization solver. Hence solver_type = 'NR'.
column96: Section 5 ('Case Study') works through a single network case: risk assessment of the proposed hyperconnected logistic hub network in the Georgia testbed (17 hubs), executed in two steps - (1) identifying risk types and the most effective tools across representative time intervals, and (2) daily 2024 risk assessments aggregated into yearly summaries with cosine-similarity-based clustering. There is no test set scored against expected answers, no user study, no controlled comparison of conditions, and no operational field deployment, so only 'single-case' applies.
column98: The case study is a researcher-run demonstration on a proposed hub network under a hypothetical deployment assumption ('assuming all hubs are deployed', Section 3); no real organisation's operating system and no real users are involved, so the episode is coded artificial per FEDS. Ambiguity note: the external data sources are real (FAF/BTS hub data, NOAA storm records, live traffic, news), which could argue for naturalistic, but the evaluated system is not in real operational use within an organisation.
column99: No standard benchmark. Case-study inputs: logistic hub network designed from the Freight Analysis Framework (FAF) database of the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics (17 hubs in the Georgia testbed); NOAA storm event records; Wikipedia summaries; real-time traffic status; news aggregation; financial data (Yahoo Finance suggested by Figure 2 toolkit); daily risk assessments for 2024.
column100: Section 3 states the hub network is designed from the FAF database (BTS) with Georgia as the testbed; Section 4 describes the tool data sources (hub data, Wikipedia, NOAA storm data, news, traffic, finance); Section 5 applies them to the Georgia hubs with daily 2024 assessments. No public benchmark or held-out test set with expected answers is used.
column102: No alternative method is applied to the same task and cases. Related Work (Section 2) only discusses prior ML/LLM approaches without running them as baselines, and the Section 5 comparison of risk-based clusters with the geographic distribution is a comparison against observed data (explicitly not a comparator per schema), so 'none' applies.
column128: No quantitative performance metrics of the framework (e.g., accuracy, quality scores, runtime, cost, token usage) are reported; searched Sections 4-6 and both figures. The numbers in Figure 3 (traffic speed 19 km/h vs 90 km/h free-flow, 107 s travel time, data confidence 1.0/1) are example raw outputs of the Traffic Status Tool, not metrics of the method, and Figure 4a shows only a cosine-similarity heatmap color scale (1.00 to -0.75) without reported similarity values. Descriptive outcomes (17 hubs, 2 clusters) are captured under sample_size and outcome_summary.
column130: The case study is designed, executed, and interpreted solely by the authors (Sections 4-5); no external testers, domain experts, or users are mentioned anywhere in the paper, so the evaluation is not independent.
column131: 17 logistic hubs in the Georgia testbed (Figure 4, hub indices 1-17); daily risk assessments per hub across 2024
column132: Section 5 states daily risk assessments were generated for each logistic hub in 2024 and aggregated into yearly summaries. The hub count of 17 is read from Figure 4's hub-index axis (1-17) rather than stated in the text. Step 1 used 'multiple representative time intervals across different seasons' (Section 5), but the number of intervals is not reported.
column137: repeated_runs: not reported anywhere (NR). llm_as_judge: false - the LLM (GPT-4o) is the method under evaluation and no LLM scores or judges the framework's outputs; clustering uses algorithmic cosine similarity (Section 5). efficiency_metrics_reported: 'no' - efficiency appears only as a design consideration (the Notebook Tool 'manages LLM token limits', Section 4; time intervals chosen to 'balance computational efficiency and prompt limitations', Section 5), with no quantitative cost, latency, or token figures for the evaluated configurations. statistical_testing: false - no significance tests or confidence intervals are reported.
column138: ["The selection of representative time intervals for risk-type identification was constrained by computational efficiency and LLM prompt limitations (Section 5).", "Implied by future work (Section 6): dynamic risk factors are not yet incorporated, the clustering methodology could be refined for more precise risk segmentation, and scalability/efficiency could be enhanced through a multi-agent system."]
column139: Section 5 explicitly states that evaluation periods 'are selected to balance computational efficiency and prompt limitations', an author-stated constraint on the evaluation. Section 6 frames remaining gaps as future extensions (dynamic risk factors, refined clustering, multi-agent system for scalability/efficiency), which imply but do not explicitly declare limitations; the second item is included with this caveat.
column140: The framework identified the most frequent risk types across the Georgia hubs (thunderstorm wind, tornado, flash flood, lightning, flood, hail, strong wind, traffic jam) and selected the NOAA Storm Data, Wikipedia Summary and Source, and Traffic Status tools as most effective for assessment. Daily 2024 risk assessments were aggregated into yearly summaries, and cosine similarity over standardized risk profiles clustered the 17 hubs into two groups: Cluster 1 (urban hubs dominated by operational risks such as traffic jams) and Cluster 2 (hubs frequently exposed to severe weather events including tornadoes and flash floods). The authors report that risk-based clusters closely align with geographic clustering, that risk exposure does not always conform to traditional geographic boundaries, and that the framework supports scalability via long-term memory and interpretability via risk explanations.
column143: The paper describes an automated pipeline in which the human only issues the initial directive and the agent then autonomously orchestrates tools, memory, and reasoning (§4: 'The process begins when the user defines tasks or directives... These prompts are then processed by the central agent, which orchestrates multiple tools, memory, and reasoning capabilities to generate insights'). No workflow step is described in which a human reviews, approves, edits, answers a system request, or otherwise acts on intermediate or final LLM output; issuing the initial query does not count per the schema. ? Borderline: in §5 the authors state 'we select the NOAA Storm Data Tool, Wikipedia Summary and Source Tool, and Traffic Status Tool as the most effective tools for this assessment' after the step-1 experiments — this is human judgment on intermediate results, but it is presented as researcher-driven experimental configuration between the two case-study phases rather than a designed HITL pattern inside the method's workflow, so it is not counted.
column149: No explicit, reusable, machine-readable domain-knowledge structure (ontology, knowledge graph, structured schema, standards encoding, relational taxonomy, code template, or mathematical model of the planning domain) is described. The integrated tools retrieve external data — hub database, Wikipedia, NOAA storm records, news, traffic, finance — that serve as input data for the analysis (§4: 'The Hub Information Extraction Tool processes structured logistic hub data, extracting key attributes'), which per schema does not count as formalization. The LLM guidance is via free-text prompts (§1: 'we design prompts that instruct LLMs to leverage these tools'), which do not count. The cosine-similarity and hierarchical clustering (§5: 'a cosine similarity measure is applied to standardized risk profiles') are generic statistical techniques, not a domain model encoding planning structure and rules. The memory/Notebook components are storage for context and results, not a formalized knowledge structure.
column155: The case study (§5) is a demonstration/walkthrough rather than an explicit, repeatable evaluation protocol. The authors 'conduct experiments using multiple representative time intervals across different seasons' to identify frequently occurring risk types and to pick the most effective tools, but no defined test items with expected outcomes, no scoring criteria or performance metrics, and no comparison against expert ground truth or benchmarks are stated. The cosine similarity matrix and clustering (§5: 'a cosine similarity measure is applied to standardized risk profiles, capturing how closely hubs align in terms of exposure to key risks') are components of the method's analysis, not metrics evaluating system performance. Per schema, a single walkthrough without defined metrics and a stated scoring procedure does not count.
column166: Information-acquisition: the agent dynamically invokes external tools at run time to gather data beyond the given hub instance (state/latitude/longitude from the FAF database), retrieving Wikipedia context, NOAA storm records, news, real-time traffic, and financial data (§4: 'The agent dynamically invokes these tools based on user instructions and data requirements, while LLMs synthesize structured and unstructured data into actionable insights'). Information-analysis: the LLM integrates and interprets structured and unstructured data, identifies risk types, produces daily risk assessments, aggregates them into yearly summaries, and clusters hubs by risk profile (§4-5: 'daily risk assessments for each logistic hub in 2024 are generated using the selected tools and top risk types, with the results aggregated into a comprehensive yearly summary'). Decision-selection is not coded: although the framework 'produces detailed risk assessments, feasibility classifications, and explanations for hub placement decisions' (§4), it does not rank alternatives or recommend/choose one final hub option — outputs are consistently framed as decision support ('support a structured and data-driven decision-making process for logistic hub selection', Abstract; 'support strategic decision-making in logistic hub deployment', §3). Action-implementation is absent: the system only reports assessments, classifications, and clusters; it does not write or execute any deployment decision.
column168: The system generates risk assessments, feasibility classifications, and risk-based hub clusters that human decision-makers evaluate to make the final hub deployment decision; it neither selects/ranks and presents a preferred option nor implements any decision, so it does not reach '2-recommendation'. The paper frames the framework as decision support throughout: it is built 'to support a structured and data-driven decision-making process for logistic hub selection' (Abstract), provides 'insights for risk management, resource allocation efficiency, and proactive mitigation strategies' (§1), and its clustering helps 'decision-makers... better visualize vulnerabilities and opportunities, facilitating precise resource allocation' (§5). The human evaluates these generated assessments/candidates and decides on hub deployment.
column170: Architecture is described at replication-relevant detail in Section 4: a ReAct-based agent built on LangGraph using ChatOpenAI with the gpt-4o model, seven enumerated tools (Hub Information Extraction, Wikipedia Summary and Source, Financial Data Analysis, NOAA Storm Data, News Aggregation, Traffic Status, Notebook) plus memory and reasoning components; Section 5 adds the two-step case procedure and cosine similarity on standardized risk profiles. Anchor: 'we design and implement a ReAct-based [22] framework... leveraging the LangGraph platform to integrate reasoning and action. Using ChatOpenAI with the gpt-4o model, we initialize a reasoning engine'. However, the prompts are not disclosed (only 'we design prompts that instruct LLMs to leverage these tools for assessing the feasibility of hub selection by evaluating various risk types and levels'), no decoding parameters are reported, and the clustering procedure is only named in the conclusion ('hierarchical clustering') without algorithm or parameter detail, so at least one required element for replication is missing.
column172: Category B (prototype demonstration): the framework is implemented and run on a concrete case, but no operationally defined metrics, variance, or comparators are reported, so category A's bar is not met. Section 5 shows an actual run with outputs: an example tool response for a Georgia hub (Figure 3: 'Hub Location: Latitude 33.712066, Longitude -84.236439... Risks: Traffic Jam') and a cosine-similarity heatmap plus two geographic clusters for 17 hubs (Figure 4), covering the tool-integration and risk-based-clustering claims. Partially because the run does not exercise every core claim: the scalability claim 'across multiple regions and time periods' is demonstrated on a single state ('We use Georgia as the testbed in this study'), step-1 tool selection appears researcher-driven rather than agent-driven ('we select the NOAA Storm Data Tool, Wikipedia Summary and Source Tool, and Traffic Status Tool as the most effective tools for this assessment'), and no quantitative evaluation of assessment quality is presented.
column174: No explicit failure modes of the proposed method and no threats to the validity of the evaluation itself (sample, setting, bias) are discussed. The only boundary content is future-work statements that implicitly acknowledge current limits. Anchor (Section 6): 'In the future, this work can be extended by incorporating dynamic risk factors, refining clustering methodologies for more precise risk segmentation, and proposing new hub locations based on risk-informed analysis. Additionally, integrating a multi-agent system could enhance scalability and efficiency'. A minor scope note exists ('These periods are selected to balance computational efficiency and prompt limitations', Section 5), but per the rubric this amounts to 'only future work', hence Partially.
column176: Section 2 provides a related-work review (traditional frameworks [18]; ML for SCRM: Aljohani [1], Yang et al. [21], Jahin et al. [7], Nezianya et al. [13]; LLM applications: Zhao et al. [23], Sun et al. [17]) and the introduction asserts gap claims against categories of prior methods.
